Each schedule supports:

  • weekdays: required, list of mon, tue, wed, thu, fri, sat, sun
  • start and end: optional HH:MM times

Time behavior:

  1. Omit both start and end for full-day schedule on selected weekdays.
  2. Set both start and end for a bounded window (start <= now < end).
  3. If start > end, the schedule is overnight (for example 22:00 to 06:00).
  4. Do not set only one of start or end.

Example

blocking:
  denylists:
    ads:
      - https://example.org/ads.txt
    social:
      - https://example.org/social.txt

  schedules:
    workhours:
      weekdays: [mon, tue, wed, thu, fri]
      start: "08:00"
      end: "18:00"
    nights:
      weekdays: [sun, mon, tue, wed, thu]
      start: "22:00"
      end: "06:00"
    weekend-all-day:
      weekdays: [sat, sun]

  listSchedules:
    social: [workhours, nights]

  clientGroupsBlock:
    default:
      - ads
      - social

In this example, ads is always active (no schedule mapping), while social is active during work hours or night window.

docs.title: Block type
docs.text:
You can configure, which response should be sent to the client, if a requested query is blocked. The zeroIP and custom IP modes answer only A and AAAA queries and return NXDOMAIN for other types, while nxDomain and refused apply to every query type:

blockType Example Description zeroIP zeroIP This is the default block type. Server returns 0.0.0.0 (or :: for IPv6) as result for A and AAAA queries nxDomain nxDomain return NXDOMAIN as return code refused refused return REFUSED as return code for every query type, with no answer or authority records. Caveat: stub resolvers and forwarders commonly treat REFUSED as a server failure and fall back to another configured DNS server, which bypasses blocking. custom IPs 192.100.100.15, 2001:0db8:85a3:08d3:1319:8a2e:0370:7344 comma separated list of destination IP addresses. Should contain ipv4 and ipv6 to cover all query types. Useful with running web server on this address to display the "blocked" page.

Example

blocking:
  blockType: nxDomain

docs.title: Block TTL
docs.text:
TTL for answers to blocked domains can be set to customize the time (in duration format) clients ask for those domains again. Default Block TTL is 6 hours. It applies to every blocking mode that returns records (zeroIP, nxDomain and custom IPs) and will affect how much time it could take for a client to be able to see the real IP address for a domain after receiving the blocked response.

For zeroIP and custom IP modes: The TTL is applied to the returned A/AAAA records in the answer section.

For nxDomain mode: The TTL is applied to the SOA record in the authority section. Per RFC 2308, Denyzer includes an SOA record in NXDOMAIN responses to enable proper negative caching by stub resolvers. The blockTTL value is used for both the SOA's TTL and its MINIMUM field, ensuring clients cache the NXDOMAIN response for the configured duration.

For refused mode: The response carries no answer or authority records, so blockTTL has no effect. An OPT record may still be present in the additional section for EDNS0 queries.

Example

blocking:
  blockType: 192.100.100.15, 2001:0db8:85a3:08d3:1319:8a2e:0370:7344
  blockTTL: 10s

docs.title: Lists Loading
docs.text: See Sources Loading.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Each DNS response has a TTL (Time-to-live) value. This value defines, how long is the record valid in seconds. The values are maintained by domain owners, server administrators etc. Denyzer caches the answers from all resolved queries in own cache in order to avoid repeated requests. This reduces the DNS traffic and increases the network speed, since denyzer can serve the result immediately from the cache.

With following parameters you can tune the caching behavior:

Warning

Wrong values can significantly increase external DNS traffic or memory consumption.

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description caching.minTime duration format no 0 (use TTL) How long a response must be cached (min value). If <=0, use response's TTL, if >0 use this value, if TTL is smaller caching.maxTime duration format no 0 (use TTL) How long a response must be cached (max value). If <0, do not cache responses. If 0, use TTL. If > 0, use this value, if TTL is greater caching.maxItemsCount int no 0 (unlimited) Max number of cache entries (responses) to be kept in cache (soft limit). Default (0): unlimited. Useful on systems with limited amount of RAM. caching.prefetching bool no false if true, denyzer will preload DNS results for often used queries (default: names queried more than 5 times in a 2 hour time window). Results in cache will be loaded again on their expire (TTL). This improves the response time for often used queries, but significantly increases external traffic. It is recommended to increase "minTime" to reduce the number of prefetch queries to external resolvers. caching.prefetchExpires duration format no 2h Prefetch track time window caching.prefetchThreshold int no 5 Name queries threshold for prefetch caching.prefetchMaxItemsCount int no 0 (unlimited) Max number of domains to be kept in cache for prefetching (soft limit). Default (0): unlimited. Useful on systems with limited amount of RAM. caching.cacheTimeNegative duration format no 30m Time how long negative results (NXDOMAIN response or empty result) are cached. A value of -1 will disable caching for negative results. caching.exclude Regex list no Exclusions rules as regex expressions of domains that won't be cached at all. Such as: /lan$/ or /^.*.host.com$/

Example

caching:
  minTime: 5m
  maxTime: 30m
  exclude:
    - /.*\.lan$/
    - /.*\.local$/
    - /.*\.host\.com\.(jp|fr)$/

docs.title: Loading secrets from files
docs.text:
A configuration value can be loaded from a file instead of being written inline. Currently queryLog.target supports this. Set the value to file: followed by an absolute path:

queryLog:
  target: file:/run/secrets/querylog_path

The file's contents become the value (a single trailing newline is stripped). This suits Docker/Kubernetes secrets and lets you restrict access to each secret with file permissions.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
Denyzer can collect in-memory statistics over a rolling 24h window and serve them as JSON at GET /api/stats. To use this feature, the HTTP listener must be enabled (see Basic Configuration).

The endpoint returns curated totals (summary), raw per-type breakdowns (response type, query type and response code), a per-hour time series, top-20 domains / blocked-domains / clients, and current list and cache gauges. Disabled by default; when disabled, GET /api/stats returns HTTP 503.

Parameter Mandatory Default value Description statistics.enable no false If true, enables in-memory statistics and the /api/stats endpoint

Example

statistics:
  enable: true

Note

Clients are identified by their resolved name (see client name lookup) and fall back to their IP when no name is available. Queries dropped by the rate limiter are always attributed to the client IP: the limiter runs before the client name lookup, so that its bucket key stays the connection's source IP.

docs.title: HTTP/3 (DoH3)
docs.text:
Serve DNS-over-HTTPS over HTTP/3 (RFC 9114). When enabled, Denyzer listens on UDP at the same addresses as ports.https and answers only the configured DoH endpoint (default /dns-query). Management pages, API and debug routes are never available over HTTP/3.

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description http3.enable boolean no false Enable the HTTP/3 listener. Requires ports.https to be set.

Notes:

  • The HTTP/3 listener uses TLS 1.3 (mandated by RFC 9001). The minTlsServeVersion config does not affect it.
  • If http3.enable is true but ports.https is empty, Denyzer logs a warning at startup and does not open any UDP listeners.
  • If ports.proxyProtocol includes https, HTTP/3 is disabled because QUIC/UDP cannot carry a PROXY protocol header.
  • When HTTP/3 is enabled, HTTPS responses include an Alt-Svc: h3=... header so capable clients can switch transports automatically.

Example:

ports:
  https: 443
http3:
  enable: true

docs.title: Query logging
docs.text:
You can enable the logging of DNS queries (question, answer, client, duration etc.) to a local embedded SQLite database or the console.

Warning

Query database contains sensitive information. Please ensure to inform users, if you log their queries.

docs.title: Query log types
docs.text:
You can select one of following query log types:

  • sqlite: log each query in a local embedded SQLite database file (no external database needed). This is the default when type is omitted.
  • console: log into console output. The dashboard has no data in this mode.
  • none: do not log any queries

The dashboard reads the SQLite metrics, so only the sqlite type feeds it. Because sqlite is the default, a minimal configuration only needs queryLog.target:

queryLog:
  target: /var/lib/denyzer/querylog.db

queryLog.target is required for the sqlite type. If it is left empty, Denyzer falls back to console logging instead of creating a database.

docs.title: SQLite query log
docs.text:
The sqlite target stores the query log and the dashboard metrics in a single local SQLite database (set via queryLog.target, e.g. /var/lib/denyzer or /var/lib/denyzer/denyzer.db) — no external database is required. Denyzer creates the database and its parent directory automatically.

queryLog.target accepts either a database file path or a directory. When it points at a directory (or ends with a path separator), the database is stored as <directory>/denyzer.db, which keeps a mounted Docker volume or systemd state directory working without naming the file.

Set queryLog.target to a plain filesystem path. Do not prefix it with file: — for query-log targets that prefix means "read the target value from this file" (see the secrets tip), so file:/var/lib/denyzer/querylog.db would be treated as a file to read the path from, not as the database itself.

When running in Docker, mount the directory (not just the database file) as a volume so the database persists, and include the whole directory in any backup. The database uses WAL mode, so a consistent backup must include denyzer.db, denyzer.db-wal and denyzer.db-shm (copy them while Denyzer is stopped, or use VACUUM INTO 'backup.db').

Retention (queryLog.retention.historyMonths) keeps the query history for a number of months. The default is 1 month and the supported range is 1 to 12 months. The cleanup removes the query log rows and the short-lived metric buckets (minute, hour, and the per-entity daily buckets) that are older than the selected cutoff. The all-time counters and the global daily metrics are always preserved, so the totals and the long-term history survive a cleanup.

Hint

The retention window is also used by the Purge Logs button in the dashboard's Operations card, which lets you pick the cutoff at runtime.

The dashboard keeps the 7-day and 30-day Top lists in two internal per-entity rollups inside the same metrics table. They are maintained incrementally by the query log writer (once at start-up and then hourly), so no configuration is needed. Right after an upgrade from an older database the rollups are rebuilt once by scanning the daily buckets; until that one-off rebuild finishes the Top lists fall back to the daily buckets, which is slower but returns the same numbers. The rollup rows are never removed by the retention cleanup.

docs.title: Query log fields
docs.text:
You can choose which information from processed DNS request and response should be logged in the target system. You can define one or more of following fields:

  • clientIP: origin IP address from the request
  • clientName: resolved client name(s) from the origins request
  • responseReason: reason for the response (e.g. from which upstream resolver), response type and code. For blocked queries the reason also names the matched rule per group, e.g. BLOCKED (ads: *.docler.com), so you can tell which denylist entry caused the block
  • responseAnswer: returned DNS answer
  • question: DNS question from the request
  • duration: request processing time in milliseconds

Hint

If not defined, denyzer will log all available information.

Configuration parameters:

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description queryLog.type enum (sqlite, console, none (see above)) no sqlite Type of logging target; sqlite when omitted queryLog.target string no SQLite database file path, or a directory that stores it as denyzer.db (supports file: — see Loading secrets from files) queryLog.retention.historyMonths int no 1 delete the query logs and the short-lived metrics older than N months (1-12); the all-time counters and the global daily metrics are preserved queryLog.creationAttempts int no 3 Max attempts to create specific query log writer queryLog.creationCooldown duration format no 2s Time between the creation attempts queryLog.fields list enum (clientIP, clientName, responseReason, responseAnswer, question, duration) no all which information should be logged queryLog.flushInterval duration format no 30s Interval to write buffered entries in bulk to the database queryLog.batchSize int no 100 Max entries buffered before a flush is triggered queryLog.ignore.sudn bool no false if true, queries answered as Special Use Domain Names (SUDN) are not logged queryLog.ignore.domains list of string no domains excluded from the query log; each entry is matched against the query name as an exact domain, a *.wildcard, or a /regex/ (exact domains and wildcards are stored as hashes, see Storage of entries)

Hint

Please ensure, that the database directory is writable. If you use docker, please ensure, that the directory is properly mounted (e.g. volume)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example

SQLite database with limited logging information

queryLog:
  target: /var/lib/denyzer/querylog.db
  retention:
    historyMonths: 1
  fields:
  - clientIP
  - duration
  flushInterval: 30s

Example

Ignore noisy domains

queryLog:
  target: /var/lib/denyzer/querylog.db
  ignore:
    sudn: true
    domains:
      - "*._dns-sd._udp.home"
      - "db._dns-sd._udp.home"
      - "/\\.in-addr\\.arpa$/"
      - "apple.com"

docs.title: Hosts file
docs.text:
You can enable resolving of entries, located in local hosts file.

Configuration parameters:

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description hostsFile.sources list of string no Host files (e.g. /etc/hosts on Linux) hostsFile.hostsTTL duration (no units is minutes) no 1h TTL hostsFile.filterLoopback bool no false Filter loopback addresses (127.0.0.0/8 and ::1) hostsFile.loading no See Sources Loading

Example

hostsFile:
  sources:
    - /etc/hosts
  hostsTTL: 1h
  loading:
    refreshPeriod: 30m
    strategy: fast

docs.title: Deliver EDE codes as EDNS0 option
docs.text:
DNS responses can be extended with EDE codes according to RFC8914.

For blocked queries the EDE extra text carries the same reason as the query log, including the matched group and rule (e.g. BLOCKED CNAME (ads: *.docler.com)), so a client that requests EDE information learns which denylist entry caused the block.

Configuration parameters:

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description ede.enable bool no false If true, DNS responses are delivered with EDE codes

Example

ede:
  enable: true

docs.title: EDNS Client Subnet options
docs.text:
EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) configuration parameters:

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description ecs.useAsClient bool no false Use ECS information if it is present with a netmask is 32 for IPv4 or 128 for IPv6 as CientIP ecs.forward bool no false Forward ECS option to upstream ecs.ipv4Mask int no 0 Add ECS option for IPv4 requests if mask is greater than zero (max value 32) ecs.ipv6Mask int no 0 Add ECS option for IPv6 requests if mask is greater than zero (max value 128)

Example

ecs:
  ipv4Mask: 32
  ipv6Mask: 128

docs.title: Special Use Domain Names
docs.text:
SUDN (Special Use Domain Names) are always enabled by default as they are required by various RFCs. Some RFCs have optional recommendations, which are configurable as described below. However, you can completely deactivate the blocking of SUDN by setting enable to false. Warning! You should only disable this if your upstream DNS server is local, as it shouldn't be disabled for remote upstreams.

This also covers RFC 9462 (Discovery of Designated Resolvers): queries for any name in resolver.arpa. (e.g. _dns.resolver.arpa.) are answered locally with NODATA and never forwarded upstream. Without this, stub resolvers (notably recent iOS/Android) can pick up a DDR answer from the upstream and silently upgrade to that upstream, bypassing denyzer.

Configuration parameters:

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description specialUseDomains.rfc6762-appendixG bool no true Block TLDs listed in RFC 6762 Appendix G enable bool no true completely disable or enable SUDN blocking

Example

specialUseDomains:
  rfc6762-appendixG: true

Example

specialUseDomains:
  enable: false

docs.title: DNSSEC validation
docs.text: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) provides cryptographic authentication of DNS data to protect against cache poisoning, man-in-the-middle attacks, and DNS spoofing. When enabled, Denyzer validates DNSSEC signatures on DNS responses and ensures the chain of trust from the root zone to the queried domain.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When DNSSEC validation is enabled, Denyzer will:

  • Set the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit on all upstream queries to request DNSSEC records
  • Validate cryptographic signatures (RRSIG records) in DNS responses
  • Verify the chain of trust from root to the queried domain using DNSKEY and DS records
  • Validate authenticated denial of existence using NSEC/NSEC3 records for NXDOMAIN and NODATA responses
  • Validate wildcard expansions according to RFC 4035 §5.3.4
  • Return SERVFAIL for responses with invalid DNSSEC signatures (Bogus)
  • Set the Authenticated Data (AD) flag only after successful validation
  • Add Extended DNS Error (EDE) codes per RFC 8914 when validation fails

Independently of this setting, Denyzer normalizes every response against the DNSSEC-related bits of the query it answers, because the client's DO bit is not necessarily the one used towards the upstream:

  • The DNSSEC records (RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS, NSEC, NSEC3) are stripped from the response of a client that did not set the DO bit, unless that client explicitly queried for one of those types or sent an ANY query (RFC 4035 §3.2.1, RFC 3225 §3). Validation is unaffected: the DO bit is still set towards the upstream
  • The DO bit of the query is copied into the response (RFC 3225 §3)
  • The AD flag is only reported to clients that asked for the validation result by setting the DO or AD bit (RFC 6840 §5.8)

docs.title: RFC Compliance
docs.text:
Denyzer's DNSSEC implementation complies with the following RFCs:

  • RFC 4033/4034/4035 (DNSSEC core specifications): Fully implemented
  • RFC 5155 (NSEC3): Implemented with configurable iteration limits
  • RFC 6840 (DNSSEC clarifications): Implemented including algorithm downgrade protection
  • RFC 8624 (Algorithm implementation requirements): Supports recommended algorithms
  • RFC 8914 (Extended DNS Errors): Provides detailed error information

docs.title: Security Benefits
docs.text:
DNSSEC validation protects against:

  • Cache poisoning attacks: Prevents attackers from injecting false DNS records into the cache
  • Man-in-the-middle attacks: Ensures DNS responses haven't been tampered with in transit
  • DNS spoofing: Verifies that DNS responses come from authoritative sources
  • Forged denial-of-existence: Validates that NXDOMAIN responses are authentic

docs.title: Configuration Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description dnssec.validate bool no false Enable DNSSEC validation dnssec.maxChainDepth uint no 10 Maximum domain label depth for chain of trust validation (DoS protection) dnssec.cacheExpirationHours uint no 1 How long to cache validation results in hours dnssec.maxUpstreamQueries uint no 30 Maximum upstream DNS queries per validation request (DoS protection) dnssec.maxNSEC3Iterations uint no 150 Maximum NSEC3 hash iterations allowed (DoS protection, per RFC 5155 §10.3) dnssec.clockSkewToleranceSec uint no 3600 Clock skew tolerance in seconds for signature validation (per RFC 6781 §4.1.2) dnssec.trustAnchors string array no [] Custom trust anchors (DNSKEY or DS records). Empty array uses built-in root trust anchors

docs.title: DoS Protection
docs.text:
DNSSEC validation can be computationally expensive and requires additional DNS queries. Denyzer includes several protections against DoS attacks:

  • maxChainDepth: Limits validation depth for deeply nested domains (e.g., prevents validation of a.b.c.d.e.f.g.h.i.j.example.com)
  • maxUpstreamQueries: Limits the number of upstream queries (DNSKEY/DS lookups) per validation to prevent query amplification
  • maxNSEC3Iterations: Limits NSEC3 hash iterations to prevent CPU exhaustion attacks
  • Validation caching: Caches validation results to avoid repeated expensive validations

docs.title: Clock Skew Tolerance
docs.text:
DNSSEC signatures have inception and expiration timestamps. Denyzer validates that the current time falls within this validity window. However, in real-world deployments, system clocks may not be perfectly synchronized, which can cause valid signatures to be rejected.

The clockSkewToleranceSec parameter (default: 3600 seconds = 1 hour) allows validation to succeed even if the system clock is off by the specified amount. This matches the behavior of industry-standard validators like Unbound and BIND.

Common scenarios where clock skew tolerance is important:

  • Virtual machines: Clock drift after suspend/resume or snapshot restore operations
  • Containers: Clock synchronization issues with the host system
  • IoT/embedded devices: Systems without NTP or with battery-backed RTCs that lose time
  • Systems during NTP sync: Time adjustment in progress when DNSSEC validation is needed
  • Raspberry Pi and similar SBCs: Devices that lose time on power loss

Recommended values:

  • 300 seconds (5 minutes): Conservative setting, handles typical NTP drift
  • 3600 seconds (1 hour): Default, handles timezone/DST issues and matches Unbound/BIND
  • 7200 seconds (2 hours): Lenient setting for systems with significant clock problems

Security vs. Robustness Tradeoff

Larger clock skew tolerance values increase the risk of accepting signatures that are actually expired or not yet valid. Smaller values increase the risk of false negatives from clock drift. For production deployments, ensure NTP or systemd-timesyncd is properly configured and use the default 1-hour tolerance.

docs.title: Validation Results
docs.text:
Denyzer classifies DNSSEC validation results into four categories:

Result Description Response Handling Secure Valid DNSSEC signatures and complete chain of trust AD flag set, response returned Insecure Domain is not signed with DNSSEC (no RRSIG records) AD flag cleared, response returned Bogus Invalid DNSSEC signatures or broken chain of trust SERVFAIL returned with EDE code 6 (DNSSEC Bogus), response type BOGUS Indeterminate Validation could not be completed (e.g., network errors, budget exceeded) AD flag cleared, response returned

A BOGUS result means denyzer could not obtain a trustworthy answer, so it counts as an error in the statistics — not as a block. A domain whose operator has misconfigured DNSSEC is not something denyzer blocked, and never appears in topBlockedDomains.

Upgrading

Validation failures previously used the BLOCKED response type, which counted them as blocks and reported them to clients as Extended DNS Error 15 (Blocked) instead of 6 (DNSSEC Bogus). Query log rows written before the upgrade keep the old value, so a dashboard grouping by response type shows BLOCKED and BOGUS side by side for the retention period.

docs.title: Trust Anchors
docs.text: By default, Denyzer uses the latest IANA root trust anchors (KSK-2017 and KSK-2024) for DNSSEC validation. These are the same trust anchors used by major DNS resolvers and are embedded in the Denyzer binary.

docs.title: Custom Trust Anchors
docs.text:
You can override the default trust anchors for:

  • Testing DNSSEC in lab environments
  • Validating private/internal DNSSEC-signed zones
  • Using specific trust anchors for organizational requirements

Trust anchors can be specified in two formats:

  1. DNSKEY format: Full DNSKEY record in zone file format
  2. DS format: DS record pointing to a DNSKEY in the child zone

Warning

Specifying custom trust anchors replaces the default root trust anchors. If you need to validate both public domains and private zones, you must include both the root trust anchors and your custom anchors.

docs.title: Supported Algorithms
docs.text:
Denyzer supports the following DNSSEC algorithms per RFC 8624:

Algorithm ID Status Security Level RSASHA1 5 Deprecated (still supported) Weak RSASHA256 8 Recommended Moderate RSASHA512 10 Recommended Moderate ECDSAP256SHA256 13 Recommended Strong ECDSAP384SHA384 14 Recommended Strong ED25519 15 Recommended Very Strong ED448 16 Recommended Strongest

Denyzer automatically selects the strongest available algorithm when multiple signatures are present, providing protection against algorithm downgrade attacks per RFC 6840 §5.11.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
DNSSEC validation adds overhead to DNS resolution:

  • Additional queries: Each validation may require 2-4 additional queries for DNSKEY and DS records
  • Cryptographic operations: Signature verification requires CPU time
  • Caching helps significantly: The validation cache reduces overhead for frequently queried domains

Recommendations:

  • Start with cacheExpirationHours: 1 and increase if validation overhead is acceptable
  • Consider disabling for high-volume recursive resolvers if performance is critical

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Basic DNSSEC validation

dnssec:
  validate: true

This enables DNSSEC validation with all default settings. Denyzer will validate all DNSSEC-signed domains using the built-in root trust anchors.

DNSSEC validation with custom DoS protection

dnssec:
  validate: true
  maxChainDepth: 15
  maxUpstreamQueries: 50
  maxNSEC3Iterations: 100
  cacheExpirationHours: 2

This configuration increases the allowed chain depth and upstream queries for complex delegation scenarios, while reducing NSEC3 iterations for better DoS protection and doubling the cache duration.

DNSSEC validation with clock skew tolerance for embedded systems

dnssec:
  validate: true
  clockSkewToleranceSec: 7200  # 2 hours tolerance for systems with clock drift

This configuration is suitable for embedded devices, Raspberry Pi, or systems without reliable NTP. The 2-hour tolerance allows validation to succeed even with significant clock drift, while still providing DNSSEC security.

DNSSEC validation with custom trust anchor for private zone

dnssec:
  validate: true
  trustAnchors:
    # Root KSK-2024 (required for public domains)
    - ". 172800 IN DNSKEY 257 3 8 AwEAAaz/tAm8yTn4Mfeh5eyI96WSVexTBAvkMgJzkKTOiW1vkIbzxeF3..."
    # Custom DNSKEY for internal zone
    - "corp.internal. 86400 IN DNSKEY 257 3 13 mdsswUyr3DPW132mOi8V9xESWE8jTo0dxCjjnopKl+GqJxpVXckHAeF..."

This configuration validates both public internet domains (using the root trust anchor) and a private corp.internal zone using a custom trust anchor.

Testing DNSSEC validation

dnssec:
  validate: true
log:
  level: debug

Enable debug logging to see detailed DNSSEC validation information for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem: All DNSSEC-signed domains return SERVFAIL

  • Check that your upstream DNS servers support DNSSEC and return DNSSEC records
  • Verify the DO bit is being set on upstream queries (check logs with log.level: debug)
  • Ensure your upstream servers are not stripping DNSSEC records

Problem: Specific domain fails DNSSEC validation

  • Check if the domain's DNSSEC is properly configured using online validators like DNSViz or Verisign DNSSEC Debugger
  • Enable debug logging to see detailed validation failure reasons
  • Check for expired RRSIG records or missing DNSKEY records

Problem: High CPU usage after enabling DNSSEC

  • Increase cacheExpirationHours to reduce validation frequency
  • Lower maxNSEC3Iterations if validating many NSEC3-signed zones
  • Consider disabling DNSSEC validation for internal-only resolvers

Problem: Validation fails with "budget exhausted"

  • Increase maxUpstreamQueries for domains with complex delegation chains
  • Check if upstream servers are slow to respond (may require multiple retries)
  • Increase maxChainDepth for deeply nested subdomains

Problem: Signatures rejected as "expired" or "not yet valid" despite being valid

  • Check your system clock is synchronized with NTP (timedatectl status on Linux)
  • Increase clockSkewToleranceSec if your system has known clock drift issues (VMs, containers, embedded devices)
  • Verify RRSIG inception/expiration times are reasonable using online validators
  • For systems without NTP, consider using a larger tolerance (e.g., 7200 seconds = 2 hours)

docs.title: DNS64
docs.text: DNS64 (RFC 6147) enables IPv6-only clients to access IPv4-only services by synthesizing AAAA (IPv6) records from A (IPv4) records. This technology is critical for IPv6-only networks such as cellular networks, IoT deployments, modern datacenters, and enterprise networks transitioning to IPv6.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When DNS64 is enabled, Denyzer will:

  • Intercept AAAA queries and check if native IPv6 records exist
  • If no native AAAA records are found, query for A records
  • Synthesize AAAA records by embedding IPv4 addresses into configured IPv6 prefixes
  • Return synthesized AAAA records with proper TTL and DNSSEC handling
  • Preserve CNAME/DNAME chains in synthesized responses
  • Skip synthesis if AAAA records already exist (unless they're in the exclusion set)

NAT64 Required

DNS64 requires a NAT64 gateway in your network. DNS64 alone won't enable IPv6-only clients to reach IPv4 destinations. The DNS64 prefix must match your NAT64 gateway's configuration.

docs.title: RFC Compliance
docs.text:
Denyzer's DNS64 implementation complies with:

  • RFC 6147 (DNS64 specification): Non-validating mode implementation
  • RFC 6052 (IPv4-to-IPv6 address embedding): All six prefix lengths supported (/32, /40, /48, /56, /64, /96)
  • RFC 8914 (Extended DNS Errors): Synthesized responses include EDE code 4 (Forged Answer)

docs.title: Configuration Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description dns64.enable bool no false Enable DNS64 synthesis dns64.prefixes array of CIDR no [64:ff9b::/96] IPv6 prefixes for synthesis. Valid lengths: /32, /40, /48, /56, /64, /96 (per RFC 6052) dns64.exclusionSet array of CIDR no [::ffff:0:0/96, ::1/128, fe80::/10] + prefixes Custom exclusion set. Advanced use only - overrides default exclusion behavior

docs.title: DNS64 Prefixes
docs.text:
DNS64 uses IPv6 prefixes to embed IPv4 addresses. RFC 6052 defines six valid prefix lengths, each with different bit layouts:

Prefix Length Bits Used IPv4 Position Example Prefix Example Synthesis /96 96 bits 96-127 64:ff9b::/96 192.0.2.1 → 64:ff9b::192.0.2.1 /64 64 bits 72-103 2001:db8::/64 192.0.2.1 → 2001:db8::c000:201 /56 56 bits 56-63, 72-95 2001:db8::/56 192.0.2.1 → 2001:db8:c0:0:201:: /48 48 bits 48-63, 72-87 2001:db8::/48 192.0.2.1 → 2001:db8:0:c000:2:100:: /40 40 bits 40-63, 72-79 2001:db8::/40 192.0.2.1 → 2001:db8:c0:2:1:: /32 32 bits 32-63 2001:db8::/32 192.0.2.1 → 2001:db8:c000:201::

Well-known prefix (default): 64:ff9b::/96 is the RFC 6052 well-known prefix, recommended for most deployments.

Multiple prefixes: You can configure multiple prefixes for load balancing across multiple NAT64 gateways. DNS64 will synthesize one AAAA record per prefix per A record.

Prefix Overlap Validation

Denyzer validates that configured prefixes do not overlap. Overlapping prefixes will cause startup failure.

docs.title: Exclusion Set
docs.text: DNS64 will not synthesize AAAA records if the response already contains AAAA records that are not in the exclusion set. This prevents synthesizing for domains that already have native IPv6 support.

docs.title: Default Exclusion Set (Recommended)
docs.text:
If dns64.exclusionSet is not configured, Denyzer uses the default exclusion set:

  • IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (::ffff:0:0/96) - RFC 6147 requirement
  • Loopback address (::1/128) - RFC 6147 recommendation
  • Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) - RFC 6147 recommendation
  • Unspecified address (::/128) - Special case
  • Configured DNS64 prefixes - Automatically added to prevent synthesis loops

Example: If a domain returns AAAA record 2001:db8::1 (not in exclusion set), DNS64 will not synthesize. If a domain returns only ::1 (in exclusion set), DNS64 will synthesize from A records.

docs.title: Custom Exclusion Set (Advanced)
docs.text:
Advanced Configuration

Configuring a custom exclusion set is an advanced feature and should only be used if you understand DNS64 synthesis behavior. Most users should use the default exclusion set.

You can configure a custom exclusion set using the dns64.exclusionSet parameter:

Example

dns64:
  enable: true
  prefixes:
    - 64:ff9b::/96
  exclusionSet:
    - ::ffff:0:0/96  # IPv4-mapped (REQUIRED by RFC)
    - ::1/128        # Loopback (recommended)
    - fe80::/10      # Link-local (recommended)
    - 64:ff9b::/96   # Your configured prefix (recommended to prevent loops)
    - 2001:db8::/32  # Custom exclusion range

Important: No Automatic Prefix Addition

When using a custom exclusion set, configured DNS64 prefixes are NOT automatically added. You must explicitly include your configured prefixes in the exclusion set to prevent synthesis loops.

Bad configuration (will cause synthesis loops): 

dns64:
  prefixes:
    - 64:ff9b::/96
  exclusionSet:
    - ::ffff:0:0/96  # Missing configured prefix!

Good configuration: 

dns64:
  prefixes:
    - 64:ff9b::/96
  exclusionSet:
    - ::ffff:0:0/96
    - 64:ff9b::/96   # Includes configured prefix

docs.title: DNSSEC Handling (Non-Validating Mode)
docs.text:
DNS64 operates in non-validating mode and handles DNSSEC as follows:

  • DO bit: Copied from original AAAA query to A query (preserves client's DNSSEC request)
  • CD bit: Copied from original AAAA query to A query (preserves checking-disabled flag)
  • AD bit: Always cleared in synthesized responses (synthesis breaks authentication)
  • Extended DNS Error: Synthesized responses include EDE code 4 (Forged Answer)

Future: DNSSEC-Aware DNS64

Future enhancement may implement RFC 6147 Section 3 (DNSSEC-aware operation), where DNS64 can validate DNSSEC signatures and set the AD bit appropriately for synthesized responses. The current non-validating mode is suitable for most deployments.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
DNS64 adds overhead to DNS resolution:

  • Additional A query: Every AAAA query that requires synthesis triggers an additional A query
  • Caching is critical: Enable caching to minimize upstream query load
  • Cache hit rate: With caching, most AAAA queries hit the cache and avoid synthesis overhead

Enable Caching for DNS64

DNS64 without caching will double upstream query load (one AAAA + one A per query). Denyzer will log a warning if DNS64 is enabled without caching.

docs.title: Healthcheck
docs.text:
Denyzer responds to a dedicated healthcheck.denyzer DNS query that is designed for container liveness probes. The handler is registered on the DNS listeners created by Denyzer (UDP, TCP, DoT) and responds to any query type with NOERROR and an empty answer section. It does not go through the resolver chain, so it stays cheap and is unaffected by upstream health.

Example

dig @<denyzer-host> -p <dns-port> healthcheck.denyzer A +short

Returns no answer records but status: NOERROR — probes should test for status: NOERROR, not for any record content.

Docker / Kubernetes liveness probe

A liveness probe should treat a NOERROR response as healthy. The image ships no dig, so use the built-in healthcheck command instead of shelling out to a DNS client. Example for Docker Compose:

healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD", "/app/denyzer", "healthcheck"]
  interval: 30s
  timeout: 5s
  retries: 3

The same command works as a Kubernetes liveness probe:

livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["/app/denyzer", "healthcheck"]
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 30
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Sources are a concept shared by the blocking and hosts file resolvers. They represent where to load the files for each resolver.

The supported source types are:

  • HTTP(S) URL (any source starting with http)
  • inline configuration (any source containing a newline)
  • local file path (any source not matching the above rules)

Note

The format/content of the sources depends on the context: lists and hosts files have different, but overlapping, supported formats.

Example

- https://example.com/a/source # denyzer will download and parse the file
- /a/file/path # denyzer will read the local file
- | # denyzer will parse the content of this multi-line string
  # inline configuration

docs.title: Sources Loading
docs.text:
This section covers loading configuration that applies to both the blocking and hosts file resolvers, except groupConcurrency, which applies only to blocking lists. These settings apply only to the resolver under which they are nested.

Example

blocking:
  loading:
    # only applies to allow/denylists

hostsFile:
  loading:
    # only applies to hostsFile sources

docs.title: Refresh / Reload
docs.text:
To keep source contents up-to-date, denyzer can periodically refresh and reparse them. Default period is 4 hours. You can configure this by setting the refreshPeriod parameter to a value in duration format. A value of zero or less will disable this feature.

Example

loading:
  refreshPeriod: 1h

Refresh every hour.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Configures how HTTP(S) sources are downloaded:

Parameter Type Mandatory Default value Description timeout duration no 5s Download attempt timeout writeTimeout duration no 20s File write attempt timeout readTimeout duration no 20s Download request read timeout readHeaderTimeout duration no 20s Download request header read timeout attempts int no 3 How many download attempts should be performed cooldown duration no 500ms Time between the download attempts cachePath path no (empty) Directory for an on-disk cache of downloaded sources (see below)

cachePath (default: empty): directory for an on-disk cache of downloaded sources. When set, denyzer sends HTTP conditional requests (If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since) and skips re-downloading unchanged lists, serves a source from disk when its host is temporarily unreachable, and — with loading.strategy: fast — seeds lists from disk on startup so it can answer queries immediately. Validators are kept in memory and reset on restart, so the first refresh after a restart re-downloads each source. When unset, downloads are fully stateless (nothing is written to disk). Mount this directory on a persistent volume in containerized setups. Note: when you remove or change a source URL, its previous cache file is left on disk — denyzer does not delete orphaned cache files automatically. They are harmless and bounded; clear the cache directory manually if you want to reclaim the space.

The directory must be writable by denyzer

If denyzer cannot write to cachePath, it logs cannot create temp cache file in <path>, serving without caching and keeps resolving normally — only the on-disk cache is disabled, so this degrades performance rather than breaking DNS.

In Docker, denyzer runs as UID 100. Use the pre-created /app/cache directory with a named volume, or make your own path writable by UID 100. See writable mounts and file permissions.

Example

loading:
  downloads:
    timeout: 4m
    attempts: 5
    cooldown: 10s
    cachePath: /var/cache/denyzer/lists

In a container, prefer the pre-created cache directory and mount a named volume over it (-v denyzer_cache:/app/cache):

loading:
  downloads:
    cachePath: /app/cache

docs.title: Strategy
docs.text:
See Init Strategy. In this context, "init" is loading and parsing each source, and an error is a single source failing to load/parse.

Example

loading:
  strategy: failOnError

docs.title: Max Errors per Source
docs.text:
Number of errors allowed when parsing a source before it is considered invalid and parsing stops. A value of -1 disables the limit.

Example

loading:
  maxErrorsPerSource: 10

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Denyzer downloads and processes sources concurrently. This allows limiting how many can be processed in the same time. Larger values can reduce the overall list refresh time at the cost of using more RAM. Please consider reducing this value on systems with limited memory. Default value is 4.

Example

loading:
  concurrency: 10

Note

The limit applies independently to the denylist cache, the allowlist cache, and the hosts file resolver. If blocking has a limit of 8 and hosts file's is 4, there can be up to 20 concurrent source jobs (8 denylist + 8 allowlist + 4 hosts file).

docs.title: Group Concurrency
docs.text:
Denyzer loads list groups concurrently. This limits how many groups are rebuilt at the same time. Larger values reduce startup and refresh time when several groups are configured, at the cost of holding several replacement caches in memory at once.

The default is auto: one group per source concurrency slot, capped by the number of groups, i.e. min(number of groups, max(1, loading.concurrency)). Set it to 1 to rebuild one group at a time.

Example

loading:
  concurrency: 4
  groupConcurrency: 2

Note

The limit applies independently to the denylist and allowlist caches. Hosts files have no groups and ignore this setting. See Startup performance for benchmark results.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You can choose one of the following installation options:

  • Run as standalone binary
  • Run as docker container

docs.title: Prepare your configuration
docs.text:
Denyzer supports single or multiple YAML files as configuration. Create new config.yml with your configuration (see Configuration for more details and all configuration options).

Simple configuration file, which enables only basic features:

upstreams:
  groups:
    default: # (1)!
      - 46.182.19.48
      - 80.241.218.68
      - tcp-tls:fdns1.dismail.de:853
      - https://dns.digitale-gesellschaft.ch/dns-query
blocking:
  denylists:
    ads: # (2)!
      - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/StevenBlack/hosts/master/hosts
  clientGroupsBlock:
    default:
      - ads
ports:
  dns: 53 # (3)!
  admin: 4000
  1. Upstream DNS resolvers denyzer forwards allowed queries to. Plain IPs as well as tcp-tls: (DoT) and https:// (DoH) endpoints are supported.
  2. A named denylist group. Each entry is a URL or local file with hosts/domains to block; reference it from clientGroupsBlock.
  3. Listening ports — dns serves DNS (UDP/TCP), admin serves the HTTPS management API and dashboard. Optional http/https ports serve DoH only.

docs.title: Set the administrator password
docs.text:
After downloading the binary, set credentials before starting this configuration:

./denyzer auth --config config.yml --username admin

The command prompts twice without echoing the password and atomically writes an Argon2id hash with file permissions 0600. Use the same command to reset the password. The server user must be able to read the resulting file; the CLI user needs write access to its directory. Docker users can use the one-off command below instead.

The dashboard is at https://<denyzer-host>:4000/, with login at /login/. Configure certFile and keyFile with a trusted certificate matching this hostname/IP. The generated self-signed certificate is not trusted by default, may not match the access address, and is rejected by the CLI. See Management authentication.

docs.title: Run Denyzer
docs.text:
Standalone binaryDocker

Download the binary file from GitHub for your architecture and run ./denyzer --config config.yml.

Warning

To bind a privileged port (< 1024, e.g. 53 or 853) as a non-root user on Linux, the binary needs the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability. Add it with setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' ./denyzer, run as root (not recommended), or configure a port >= 1024.

If Denyzer runs under a restricted capability bounding set (for example a hardened systemd unit, or a container that drops capabilities), use setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+p' ./denyzer instead. Denyzer raises the capability to effective itself at startup, which avoids the operation not permitted exec error that +ep triggers when the capability is not in the bounding set.

Keep the configuration in a directory so the running container can see atomic credential replacements. Prepare credentials as the image's UID 100:

mkdir -p config
cp config.yml config/config.yml
sudo chown 100:100 config config/config.yml
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD/config:/config" mia0x75/denyzer \
  auth --config /config --username admin

Rerun the same one-off auth command to reset a running container's password. The server can keep the configuration directory mounted read-only; the one-off auth container needs the writable mount shown above. Do not mount a single config file for live resets: replacing it on the host can leave the running container reading the old inode until the container is recreated.

Running under a restricted runtime

The container image is capability-aware. The binary ships with cap_net_bind_service=+p (permitted only), so the container starts even under a restricted runtime that drops all capabilities (for example the Kubernetes Restricted Pod Security Standard, capabilities: drop: [ALL]).

  • On ports >= 1024 no capability is required.
  • On privileged ports (< 1024, e.g. 53/853) Denyzer needs NET_BIND_SERVICE. With the default runtime capability set it is already present and Denyzer enables it automatically. Under drop: [ALL], grant it back (Kubernetes securityContext.capabilities.add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"], or docker run --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE) or configure a port >= 1024.

Writable mounts and file permissions

The container runs as the unprivileged user UID 100. Any directory Denyzer writes to - the query log target, or loading.downloads.cachePath - must be writable by that user, otherwise Denyzer logs a permission denied error and continues without writing.

The image ships /app/cache and /logs pre-created and owned by UID 100, so mounting a named volume over either path works with no host-side setup:

docker run -v denyzer_cache:/app/cache ... mia0x75/denyzer

A bind mount always keeps the host directory's ownership, so it needs one of:

  • chown -R 100:100 /path/on/host before starting the container, or
  • run as the host user that owns the directory: docker run -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" ..., or in compose user: "1000:1000".

Configuration and TLS private-key files must also be readable by UID 100. The auth command writes credentials with mode 0600, so preserve the container user's ownership rather than making them world-readable.

Denyzer docker images are deployed to DockerHub (mia0x75/denyzer) and GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/mia0x75/denyzer).

docker rundocker-compose

Execute the following command from the command line:

docker run --name denyzer -v /path/to/config:/config:ro \
  -e DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE=/config -p 127.0.0.1:4000:4000 \
  -p 53:53/tcp -p 53:53/udp mia0x75/denyzer

Create the following docker-compose.yml file:

version: "2.1"
services:
  denyzer:
    image: mia0x75/denyzer
    container_name: denyzer
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Optional the instance hostname for logging purpose
    hostname: denyzer-hostname
    ports:
      - "53:53/tcp"
      - "53:53/udp"
      - "127.0.0.1:4000:4000/tcp" # HTTPS management; change the host bind for trusted LAN access
    environment:
      - DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE=/config
      - TZ=Europe/Berlin # Optional to synchronize the log timestamp with host
    volumes:
      # Optional to synchronize the log timestamp with host
      - /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro
      # config directory, prepared with the auth command above
      - ./config:/config:ro

Then start the container with:

docker-compose up -d

docs.title: Container configuration file
docs.text:
You can define the location of the config file in the container with environment variable DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE. Using this environment variable a folder containing configuration files can also be specified. Default value is /app/config.yml.

Legacy: CONFIG_FILE

Older Denyzer versions used CONFIG_FILE instead of DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE. The legacy name is still accepted as a fallback when DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE is unset. New deployments should use DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE.

docs.title: Advanced docker-compose setup
docs.text:
Following example shows, how to run denyzer in a docker container and store query logs on a SAMBA share. Local black and allowlists directories are mounted as volume. You can create own black or allowlists in these directories and define the path like '/app/allowlists/allowlist.txt' in the config file.

Example

version: "2.1"
services:
  denyzer:
    image: mia0x75/denyzer
    container_name: denyzer
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "53:53/tcp"
      - "53:53/udp"
      - "127.0.0.1:4000:4000/tcp" # HTTPS management API and dashboard
    environment:
      - DENYZER_CONFIG_FILE=/config
      - TZ=Europe/Berlin
    volumes:
      # config directory, including administrator credentials
      - ./config:/config:ro
      # write query logs in this volume
      - queryLogs:/logs
      # put your custom allow/denylists in these directories
      - ./denylists:/app/denylists/
      - ./allowlists:/app/allowlists/

volumes:
  queryLogs:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: cifs
      # uid=100 is required: the share is mounted root-owned by default and
      # Denyzer runs as UID 100, which could then not write the query logs
      o: username=USER,password=PASSWORD,uid=100,gid=100,rw
      device: //NAS_HOSTNAME/denyzer

Note

The ./denylists and ./allowlists bind mounts above are only read by Denyzer, so they need no ownership changes. See the permission note under Run Denyzer if you add a writable bind mount.

docs.title: Multiple configuration files
docs.text:
For complex setups, pass a folder containing YAML files. Denyzer recursively merges them in lexical path order; later scalar and list values override earlier ones. See Multiple configuration files.

./denyzer --config ./config/

Warning

Duplicate keys within a single YAML document are rejected. In directory mode, denyzer auth --config ./config/ --username admin updates the last YAML file.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
OpenAPI specification <pre><code>openapi: 3.1.1

  title: denyzer API
  description: >-

    DoH listeners do not expose this API. When authentication is enabled,
    every operation except GET/POST /login requires an Authorization: Bearer

    or debug requests. Tokens expire seven days after login without renewal;
    logout revokes the current session, while a password reset or restart
    invalidates all sessions. Authentication may be disabled only on explicit
    loopback management addresses.


    Protected operations return 401 for missing, expired or invalid tokens.
    Cross-origin management requests return 403, and unavailable or invalid
    authentication configuration returns 503.


    For features, configuration, and installation see the

  contact:
    name: denyzer@github

  license:
    name: Apache 2.0
    url: http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html
  version: '1.0'
servers:
  - url: /api
security:
  - bearerAuth: []
paths:

    get:
      operationId: loginStatus
      tags:
        - auth
      security: []
      summary: Check whether administrator authentication is enabled
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Authentication status
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  enabled:
                    type: boolean
                required:
                  - enabled
        '403':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/ForbiddenOrigin'
        '503':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/AuthUnavailable'
    post:
      operationId: login
      tags:
        - auth
      security: []
      summary: Log in as the single administrator
      description: >-
        Accepts a JSON body up to 8 KiB. Invalid usernames and passwords both
        return 401 invalid credentials. Login attempts are rate-limited and
        at most 128 sessions can be active. The token is opaque, not a JWT.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              additionalProperties: false
              properties:
                username:
                  type: string

                password:
                  type: string
                  format: password

                - username
                - password

        '401':

          headers:
            Set-Cookie:
              description: Clears denyzer_page_session with the same secure cookie attributes
              schema:
                type: string
        '401':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/InvalidCredentials'
        '403':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/ForbiddenOrigin'
        '503':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/AuthUnavailable'

          schema:

        - name: groups
          in: query

          schema:

        '400':
          description: Bad request (e.g. unknown group)
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:

                example: Bad request

      tags:
        - blocking

      description: enable the blocking status
      responses:

          content:

          content:

      tags:
        - cache

      responses:

          description: All caches cleared
  /stats:
    get:
      operationId: getStats
      tags:
        - stats
      summary: DNS statistics
      description: >-
        In-memory statistics over a rolling 24h window. Requires statistics to be
        enabled in the configuration; returns 503 otherwise.
        All timestamps (start, end, perHour[].hour) are returned in UTC (RFC 3339,
        `Z` suffix).
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current statistics
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/api.Stats'
        '503':
          description: Statistics are disabled
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                type: string
                example: statistics are disabled
  # --- SQLite dashboard API (embedded database) ---
  # These endpoints are served directly by the server on top of the embedded
  # SQLite store used by the DenyzerUI dashboard. They are tagged `dashboard` and
  # excluded from the generated OpenAPI client/server code (see api/*.cfg.yaml
  # `output-options.exclude-tags`), so they are kept in sync only here and in
  # server/api_handlers.go.

    get:
      operationId: dashboardStatsSummary
      tags:

      summary: All-time DNS statistics summary
      description: >-

          description: Current all-time statistics summary
          content:

              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/api.StatsSummaryResponse'
        '500':
          description: query_stats read error
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                type: string
  /stats/hourly_trend:
    get:
      operationId: dashboardStatsTrend
      tags:
        - dashboard
      summary: Query statistics trend over time
      description: >-
        Returns a zero-filled time axis of query counts, ordered oldest first.
        Granularity depends on the parameters: minute buckets are used when
        `hours <= 1`, hourly buckets otherwise, and daily buckets when `days` is
        set (the days parameter wins). Timestamps are UTC; daily rows use
        `YYYY-MM-DD`.
      parameters:
        - name: hours
          in: query
          description: Number of hourly buckets to return (default 24).
          schema:
            type: integer
            default: 24
        - name: days
          in: query
          description: >-
            If set, returns `days` daily buckets instead of hourly ones.
          schema:
            type: integer
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Trend entries, oldest first.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/api.HourlyTrendEntry'
        '500':
          description: Statistics read error
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                type: string
  /stats/top_domains:
    get:
      operationId: dashboardStatsTopDomains
      tags:
        - dashboard
      summary: Top queried domains
      description: >-
        Aggregates the per-day top_domains table over the last `days` days and
        returns the `limit` most queried domains, sorted by count descending.
        When `hours` is set it scans the query_logs detail for that rolling
        window instead (used by the "1h" dashboard view).
      parameters:
        - name: days
          in: query

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Configure the single administrator with denyzer auth --username admin (configuration details). Open https://<denyzer-host>:<admin-port>/login/ to log in; the dashboard is at / on the same HTTPS origin. Use a trusted certificate matching this hostname/IP.

GET /api/login returns {"enabled":true} or {"enabled":false} without authentication. When the request carries a valid page cookie it also returns that session's token, so a second tab or a restarted browser continues the same session. POST /api/login accepts application/json with username and password, and returns token and expiresAt. Wrong usernames and passwords both return 401 invalid credentials.

Include Authorization: Bearer <token> on all other API and debug requests. POST /api/logout revokes the current token, clears the page cookie and returns 204. Tokens expire seven days after login without renewal, and all tokens are invalidated by a password reset or server restart. Cookies authenticate pages only; the dashboard keeps its API token in sessionStorage and clears it before returning to /login/ on a 401. Transport failures, HTTP server errors and cancelled requests keep the session: a network blip does not sign the administrator out, and a regenerated self-signed certificate surfaces as a connection error telling the user to reload. Cross-origin management requests are rejected with 403. An unreadable or invalid auth configuration fails closed with 503.

Authentication can be disabled only for explicit loopback management binds, with a startup warning. Public DoH remains unauthenticated and separate.

docs.title: Common endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path Purpose GET /api/login Check whether authentication is enabled. POST /api/login Create a seven-day administrator session. POST /api/logout Revoke the current Bearer session. POST /api/blocking/enable Enable blocking globally. POST /api/blocking/disable Disable blocking globally (optional duration, groups query params). GET /api/blocking/status Return current blocking status as JSON. POST /api/lists/refresh Refresh all allow/denylists. POST /api/cache/flush Clear the entire DNS response cache. POST /api/query Run a DNS query through Denyzer and return the result as JSON. GET /api/stats In-memory DNS statistics over a rolling 24h window as JSON. Requires statistics to be enabled; returns 503 otherwise.

Flush the DNS cache

curl -X POST https://<denyzer-host>:<admin-port>/api/cache/flush \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DENYZER_API_TOKEN"

Returns HTTP 200 on success. Useful after editing customDNS or hostsFile entries that may already be cached.

Statistics semantics

For /api/stats, the summary fields are server-computed categories, so callers never interpret a raw response type:

Field Response types blocked BLOCKED + REBIND filtered FILTERED + NOTFQDN forwarded RESOLVED + CONDITIONAL cached CACHED local CUSTOMDNS + HOSTSFILE + SPECIAL + SYNTHESIZED errors BOGUS, plus queries a resolver failed outright

blocked counts only queries blocked to protect the client: denylist hits and DNS rebinding hits. Two other outcomes are deliberately kept out of it, so they cannot inflate blocked or the topBlockedDomains list:

  • Query-type filtering (e.g. AAAA via filtering.queryTypes) and non-FQDN rejections are client-requested, not protective, and are counted as filtered.
  • A DNSSEC validation failure (BOGUS) is a SERVFAIL — denyzer could not obtain a trustworthy answer — so it is a resolution error, not a block, and is counted as errors together with queries a resolver failed outright.

The blocked / filtered split also applies to the perHour series, which carries both. Together with dropped (rate-limited), the categories above partition every query, so they always add up to queries.

The lists and cache objects are point-in-time gauges (current values, not affected by the 24h window), while start/end bound the windowed fields only. All timestamps (start, end, perHour[].hour) are always returned in UTC (RFC 3339, Z suffix), regardless of the server's local time zone. Statistics are served as plain JSON.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Denyzer's management CLI uses the HTTPS REST API and takes its Bearer token from DENYZER_API_TOKEN. Set it to the token returned by POST /api/login. The CLI verifies the management certificate; there is no insecure TLS flag. Use --apiHost and --apiPort to select the management host and ports.admin port, not a DoH listener.

To run the CLI, please ensure, that denyzer DNS server is running, then execute denyzer help for help or

  • ./denyzer blocking enable to enable blocking
  • ./denyzer blocking disable to disable blocking
  • ./denyzer blocking disable --duration [duration] to disable blocking for a certain amount of time (30s, 5m, 10m30s, ...)
  • ./denyzer blocking disable --groups ads,othergroup to disable blocking only for special groups
  • ./denyzer blocking status to print current status of blocking
  • ./denyzer query <domain> execute DNS query (A) (simple replacement for dig, useful for debug purposes)
  • ./denyzer query <domain> --type <queryType> execute DNS query with passed query type (A, AAAA, MX, ...)
  • ./denyzer lists refresh reloads all allow/denylists
  • ./denyzer stats shows DNS statistics (requires statistics.enable: true)
  • ./denyzer validate [--config /path/to/config.yaml] validates configuration file
  • ./denyzer auth --username admin sets or resets credentials locally, without a running server
  • ./denyzer version prints only Version, Build time and Architecture

Tip

Pass the token into a running container with docker exec -e DENYZER_API_TOKEN denyzer ./denyzer blocking status. Its configured management host must also match a trusted certificate.

docs.title: Logging migration and performance
docs.text:
Measurement history

The tables and validation record source-branch experiments, not checks performed for this port. Resolver composition and host/tool availability may differ. Use the reproduction commands to measure the current build.

Denyzer uses Go's log/slog. The project log package owns its compatible handlers; there is no Logrus adapter or alternate logger in the request path. The Logrus comparison revision is db4735397feb308b3806a15824215c2210f857db.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Configuration retains text/JSON, stdout/stderr/syslog, timestamps, and privacy. Level names are case-insensitive: trace, debug, info, warn/warning, error, fatal, and panic. Custom slog levels retain Trace (-8), Fatal (12), and Panic (16); JSON still renders Warn as "warning".
  • JSON retains time, level, and msg, including time with timestamp: false. Conflicting user fields move to fields.time, fields.level, and fields.msg. Strings use encoding/json-compatible escaping; arbitrary values retain its marshaling and error semantics.
  • Text retains resolver prefixes, dotted sub-prefixes, sorted fields, and nested configuration indentation. Syslog receives record severity directly, without encoding it into byte markers. Failed syslog setup falls back to stderr.
  • Startup buffering snapshots events at capture time and replays them in order with the destination's configured level, format, and target. Indentation only affects text. Fatal error handling still logs and exits with status 1.
  • Existing derived loggers follow output and level reconfiguration. Switching waits for in-flight writes before closing an old syslog connection.

log/logger_compat_test.go, handler conformance tests using testing/slogtest, Buffer/Recorder tests, syslog tests, resolver field/privacy tests, and subprocess failure/fatal tests constrain these behaviors.

docs.title: Request-path design
docs.text:
Each resolver constructs its prefixed *slog.Logger once. The server attaches req_id, question, and client_ip as context attributes once per request; DebugContext, InfoContext, and LogAttrs carry them to enabled records without cloning a logger at every resolver boundary. Explicit initialization/test loggers still take precedence. Request IDs remain standard-library UUID v7.

Question values snapshot the original question before any resolver mutates it, then defer formatting and privacy filtering until emission. Answer snapshots copy mutable DNS records, so their construction is guarded with Enabled. Cold bootstrap hostname refreshes attach the originating upstream's attributes only on a cache miss, not on every query.

Deferred values and errors resolve once before capture/output fan-out. Recorder snapshots own groups, maps, slices, and collections nested in arrays, including cycles; arbitrary mutable pointers and structs are not a deep-copy API. Its records and message lists are safe to inspect concurrently. Enabled JSON output renders typed attributes directly rather than constructing a reflection-heavy map[string]any for each event.

No first-party source imports Logrus or its old formatter. Logrus remains an indirect container-test dependency, not part of the production binary.

docs.text:
Do not equate complete query allocations with logging allocations:

The baseline worktree has benchmark-only matched Logrus controls for the new cases; production source is unchanged. These controls do not ship in Denyzer.

docs.title: Network configuration
docs.text: In order, to benefit from all the advantages of denyzer like ad-blocking, privacy and speed, it is necessary to use denyzer as DNS server for your devices. You can configure DNS server on each device manually or use DHCP in your network router and push the right settings to your device. With this approach, you will configure denyzer only once in your router and each device in your network will automatically use denyzer as DNS server.

docs.title: Transparent configuration with DHCP
docs.text:
Let us assume, denyzer is installed on a Raspberry PI with fix IP address 192.168.178.2. Each device which connects to the router will obtain an IP address and receive the network configuration. The IP address of the Raspberry PI should be pushed to the device as DNS server.

┌──────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
│              │         │ Raspberry PI    │
│  Router      │         │   denyzer        │        
│              │         │ 192.168.178.2   │            
└─▲─────┬──────┘         └────▲────────────┘        
  │1    │                     │  3                  
  │     │                     │                         
  │     │                     │ 
  │     │                     │                     
  │     │                     │
  │     │                     │
  │     │                     │
  │     │       ┌─────────────┴──────┐
  │     │   2   │                    │
  │     └───────►  Network device    │
  │             │    Android         │
  └─────────────┤                    │
                └────────────────────┘

1 - Network device asks the DHCP server (on Router) for the network configuration

2 - Router assigns a free IP address to the device and says "Use 192.168.178.2" as DNS server

3 - Clients makes DNS queries and is happy to use denyzer

Warning

It is necessary to assign the server which runs denyzer (e.g. Raspberry PI) a fix IP address.

To configure the DNS server in the FritzBox, please open in the FritzBox web interface:

  • "IPv4 Configuration" Button at the bottom op the page
