docs.title: HTTPS management and public DoH
docs.text:
The management service is a separate HTTPS listener, configured with ports.admin. It serves the dashboard at /, login at /login/, and management API/debug routes. ports.http serves only HTTP DoH; ports.https and optional HTTP/3 serve only encrypted DoH. Public DoH never exposes management routes, and the management listener never answers DoH.

Set credentials with denyzer auth --username admin before exposing management outside explicit loopback IPs. Configure certFile and keyFile with a trusted certificate matching the management hostname/IP; these files are shared with DoH and DoT. The generated self-signed certificate is not trusted by default and may not match the access address. Client rejection of that certificate does not mean the server has crashed.

Keep the dashboard, login and API on the same HTTPS origin. If reverse-proxying management, use an HTTPS upstream and preserve the public Host header. Cross-origin management requests are not supported. See Management authentication.

docs.title: Running denyzer behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
When Denyzer's HTTP / DoH listener is fronted by a reverse proxy (nginx, Traefik, Caddy, HAProxy, ...), the TCP peer Denyzer sees is the proxy, not the real client. Denyzer ignores Forwarded and X-Forwarded-For: clients can forge those headers. Client groups, rate limits, upstream selection and query logs use the connection IP. All clients behind an ordinary HTTP reverse proxy therefore share the proxy's identity. To preserve client IPs, use the existing PROXY protocol support on a listener reachable only from trusted proxies.

nginx

location /dns-query {
    proxy_pass http://denyzer-backend:8080/dns-query;
}

Traefik (dynamic file config)

http:
  services:
    denyzer:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://denyzer-backend:8080"
  middlewares: {}
  # All clients use the proxy's IP unless PROXY protocol is configured.

docs.title: Running DoT/DoH behind a TCP proxy
docs.text:
For DNS-over-TLS and HTTPS passthrough, HTTP forwarding headers are not available before Denyzer handles the TLS connection. Enable the HAProxy PROXY protocol on the Denyzer listener and configure the proxy to send it.

Warning

List a listener under ports.proxyProtocol only when it is reachable only from trusted proxies. When enabled, Denyzer requires a PROXY protocol header and uses the source address from that header as the client IP.

The PROXY protocol only covers TCP listeners. HTTP/3 (QUIC/UDP) cannot carry a PROXY protocol header, so enabling https here automatically disables HTTP/3. Plain DNS-over-UDP is likewise unaffected by dns.

The http and https listeners serve DoH only. Enabling PROXY protocol makes direct connections to those DoH ports fail; clients must connect through the trusted proxy. The separate HTTPS management listener (ports.admin) does not use PROXY protocol and is unaffected.

Denyzer

ports:
  https: 443
  tls: 853
  proxyProtocol:
    - https
    - tls

nginx stream

stream {
    upstream denyzer_dot {
        server denyzer-backend:853;
    }

    server {
        listen 853;
        proxy_pass denyzer_dot;
        proxy_protocol on;
    }

    upstream denyzer_doh {
        server denyzer-backend:443;
    }

    server {
        listen 443;
        proxy_pass denyzer_doh;
        proxy_protocol on;
    }
}

docs.title: Query performance optimization plan
docs.text:
Measurement history

The tables record experiments from the source branch, including intermediate implementations. They are not fresh measurements of this branch. Use the reproduction commands to measure the current build.

This report records the original four-phase query optimization. Its Logrus logging decision and measurements are historical: the subsequent log/slog migration replaces the eager entry cloning and separates isolated logging overhead from complete-chain/query measurements.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Denyzer will continue using Go's standard-library regexp package.

The regex-engine benchmark in regex-engine-benchmark.md tested the real grouped-cache path with OISD-shaped and literal-prefix rules. go-re2 was not a win for this workload and its re2_cgo mode conflicts with the current cross-build environment. coregex is much faster for some OISD scans, but slower for other realistic patterns and has substantially higher compile and retained-memory costs. Neither result justifies a global engine replacement.

The optimization target is therefore the work around regex matching:

  1. measure the complete query path;
  2. evaluate the per-resolver logging plumbing (the initial Logrus lazy variant was rejected, see Phase 2; the later slog migration is reported separately);
  3. remove avoidable per-query allocations;
  4. reduce the number of regex calls with a semantics-preserving blocking pre-filter.

YAML work remains outside this plan.

docs.title: Original baseline and rules
docs.text:
The existing startup work is complete and documented in startup-performance.md. The query work uses the same measurement discipline:

  • Go 1.27.3;
  • Linux amd64, AMD Ryzen 7 5700U (16 threads), schedutil governor;
  • the governor stays at schedutil — pinning the cores to performance lets the package hit its power limit and collapses the throughput of the CPU-bound cases, exactly as the startup work showed;
  • the two sides of a comparison are run alternately (A, B, A, B, ...) and the median of the rounds is reported;
  • seven rounds per side, -benchtime=1s;
  • no concurrent compile, test, or benchmark process;
  • commands run with proxy variables removed:
env -u HTTP_PROXY -u HTTPS_PROXY -u http_proxy -u https_proxy \
  -u SOCKS5_PROXY <command>

At the time of these four phases, benchstat was unavailable in the build environment (no network access), so the A/B runner was a small local script: it built both sides once, ran the alternating rounds, and reported the median, the min-max spread and the delta. The raw output of every round is kept in the temporary benchmark directory. The later slog comparison uses benchstat and ten alternating pairs, not these historical timing tables.

Every phase must report ns/op, B/op, and allocs/op, and must include correctness tests. A speedup that changes blocking decisions, response data, logging output, or cancellation behavior is not acceptable.

docs.title: Noise floor
docs.text:
The host is a shared laptop: the schedutil governor moves the core frequency between roughly 1.1 GHz and 3.6 GHz, so the absolute ns/op of a CPU-bound case depends on the state of the machine at the moment of the run. The only meaningful comparison is therefore a relative one, measured in the same session.

Running the same build against itself calibrates the method. Seven rounds per side, both sides identical, server package:

Case Median ns/op Spread over 14 runs BenchmarkQueryPath/blocked_exact 16687 15817-17052 BenchmarkQueryPath/upstream_hit 16220 15522-18813 BenchmarkQueryPath/upstream_miss 279042 254508-330615 BenchmarkQueryPath/regex_only_miss 1879808 1477740-3646843

Most cases reproduce within ±5 %. The two that do not are the ones whose cost is dominated by something other than the code under test: upstream_miss includes a real UDP round trip, and regex_only_miss runs a linear scan over 1000 compiled regular expressions, which is bound by the memory layout of the compiled programs.

Two consequences follow for the rest of the plan:

  • allocs/op and B/op are more stable on the same toolchain and architecture, so they are the primary metric for the allocation work of phase 2 and phase 3;
  • the comparison that decides phase 4 has to be a same-binary comparison — the reference implementation stays in the test code as a second sub-benchmark, so both variants see the same frequency state. This is the pattern the startup benchmarks already use.

docs.title: Phase 1: establish the complete query baseline
Objective
docs.text:
Measure the end-to-end query path before changing allocation behavior. The benchmark must exercise the production composition rather than a synthetic function call:

server request entry
  -> resolver chain
  -> blocking/cache decisions
  -> mock upstream response

docs.title: Work
docs.text:
Add a BenchmarkQueryPath beside the existing server/resolver benchmarks and add focused breakdown benchmarks for the expensive sections. Use a local mock upstream and prebuilt resolver state so network and list-download time do not hide per-query work.

Measure at least these cases:

Case Purpose resolver-chain miss to mock upstream full common miss path cache hit avoid attributing upstream work to allocation changes blocked exact/wildcard domain verifies cheap blocking path regex-only miss isolates the remaining regex scan one-group and multi-group lookup exposes result-map and group-scan costs debug/trace disabled and enabled separates normal traffic from logging traffic

Record the resolver-chain depth and list sizes in the benchmark name. Keep the existing BenchmarkCachingResolverResolve and logging benchmarks as lower-level references.

docs.title: What was added
docs.text:
• server/query_path_bench_test.go — BenchmarkQueryPath (eight baseline cases, with regex_late_hit added in Phase 4), BenchmarkQueryPathLogLevel (info, debug, trace) and BenchmarkNewRequest;
  • resolver/query_path_bench_test.go — BenchmarkBlockingResolve (six cases) for the denylist lookup alone;
  • helpertest/benchdata — the shared list data. The regex-only cases use 1000 rules sampled with an even stride from the OISD list the repository ships (helpertest/data/oisd-big-wildcard.txt, 209612 wildcard entries), in the shape a real OISD-derived list has: /^(.*\.)?<domain>$/. Such a rule has no literal prefix, so the engine has to scan it.

The chain under test is the production chain of createQueryResolver: 19 resolvers, from the statistics resolver down to the upstream tree. The mock upstream is an in-process UDP server, so a query that no resolver answers locally performs a real socket round trip.

Two details of the benchmark setup are worth keeping:

  • The query names use a plain domain (query-path-bench.com). The special-use domain names (test., example., invalid., localhost.) are answered by the special-use domain resolver, which sits above the upstream tree in the chain. A query for one of them is answered locally and never reaches the upstream or the cache — the cache-hit case would silently measure the special-use path instead.
  • Every case verifies its own result before the measurement starts: the response type (RESOLVED, CACHED, BLOCKED) and, for the blocked cases, the matched rule. A case that stops measuring the path it claims to measure fails instead of reporting a wrong number.

docs.title: What the baseline shows
docs.text:
• The logging plumbing is a large per-query cost. The original 15-resolver BenchmarkChainLoggingPlumbing pays 109 allocations and 10.2 KB per request without writing a line, but also constructs the backend DNS response: these totals are not isolated logging costs. The later slog report supplies an isolated logging benchmark and retains this benchmark as a control. The complete query path costs 53 allocations (cache hit) to 180 allocations (upstream miss), so the logger rebuild is a large part of the smaller numbers. This is the target of phase 2.
  • The denylist lookup itself is cheap. One group costs 14 allocations and 1.3 KB; four groups cost 16 allocations and 1.4 KB. The per-group cost is small, but the result map that the lookup returns is allocated on every lookup — the target of phase 3.
  • The regex scan dominates everything else. With 1000 OISD-shaped rules the regex-only miss needs 1.9 ms in the complete path and 8.0 ms in the isolated lookup — more than two orders of magnitude more than the rest of the query path, and it is pure CPU time. This is the target of phase 4.
  • The upstream round trip is not the interesting cost. 180 allocations and 15.7 KB for a full miss, of which the socket exchange and the response packing are a constant part that no allocation change can remove.

docs.title: Deliverables and acceptance
docs.text:
• docs/query-performance.md updated with the baseline tables and exact commands — done;
  • raw output retained under the temporary benchmark directory — done;
  • no production behavior change — the phase only adds benchmark code and a helper package;
  • baseline can be reproduced three times on an idle host — the allocation figures are exactly reproducible, the ns/op figures are host dependent within the spread documented above;
  • benchmark checks response identity, blocking result, and error behavior — every case verifies the response type and the matched rule before it measures.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: In the original implementation, each resolver called r.log(ctx). That rebuilt a context logger and copied Logrus entry state once per resolver even when the configured level would not emit a log line. The original BenchmarkChainLoggingPlumbing measures approximately 109 allocations and 10 KB per 15-resolver request-shaped chain.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Create the request-scoped log entry once at the server boundary.
  • Preserve request fields (req_id, question, and client_ip) and the current prefix format.
  • Attach the resolver type only at a log site that is actually enabled, or use a lightweight resolver-scoped view that does not clone the request context for a disabled message.
  • Keep expensive values behind level checks. In particular, do not calculate QuestionToString, AnswerToString, obfuscated answers, or formatted error text before checking Debug/Trace enablement.
  • Keep uuid.NewV7() as the request ID generator from the Go 1.27.3 standard library migration. Do not replace the externally visible request ID format with an unrelated monotonic integer as part of this phase.

docs.title: Required tests
docs.text:
• golden tests for prefix and field output;
  • tests proving request fields survive every resolver boundary;
  • Debug and Trace enabled tests proving the same messages still appear;
  • disabled-level tests proving expensive arguments are not constructed;
  • race test for concurrent requests sharing the base logger.

docs.title: Acceptance target
docs.text:
The Phase 1 baseline gives the numbers to beat:

Measurement Baseline BenchmarkChainLoggingPlumbing (15 resolvers) 109 allocs, 10152 B BenchmarkQueryPath/upstream_hit (complete chain) 53 allocs, 4376 B BenchmarkQueryPath/blocked_exact (complete chain) 55 allocs, 4214 B BenchmarkQueryPathLogLevel/info 55 allocs, 4211 B BenchmarkQueryPathLogLevel/trace 81 allocs, 7231 B

The target is a substantial reduction of both numbers — the logging plumbing must no longer dominate the per-query allocation count, and the trace level must not cost more than the info level by a multiple. Logging output compatibility takes priority over a fixed allocation number: the golden tests have to pass unchanged.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The lazy design was dropped. It carried only the resolver prefix in the request context and materialized the prefix through a logrus hook when a line was emitted. The hook was rejected because it relies on logrus behavior that does not support it safely:

  • logrus.Logger.Hooks is a public map. AddHook/ReplaceHooks write it under the logger mutex, but the hook lookup reads it without that lock, so adding a hook to a logger that is used concurrently is a data race.
  • the prefix was applied when the line was emitted, so a nested resolver overwrote the prefix of the outer resolver and the dotted prefix chain (blocking.client_id_cache) collapsed to its first element.

This initial phase kept the eager plumbing that was in place before it: every resolver derived its entry from the request entry with log.SetPrefix, which replaces the prefix instead of accumulating it. The request fields (req_id, question, client_ip) are preserved, the prefix semantics are unchanged, and the cost is the logrus data-map clone that Entry.WithField performed - one clone per resolver per request. The clone was accepted at that checkpoint instead of adding a second logging mechanism next to Logrus. The subsequent slog migration removes this cost without retaining the rejected hook or a compatibility bridge.

The golden tests of the log package and the resolver tests cover the prefix and field output; go test -race ./log ./resolver covers the concurrent use of the shared request entry.

Phase 2 therefore contributes no allocation improvement: the plumbing is identical to the Phase 1 baseline. The numbers below were measured on the same host with -benchmem; the tiny differences in the log-level rows are the measurement noise of the byte counter.

Measurement Phase 1 Phase 2 BenchmarkChainLoggingPlumbing (15 resolvers) 109 allocs, 10152 B 109 allocs, 10152 B BenchmarkQueryPath/upstream_hit 53 allocs, 4376 B 53 allocs, 4376 B BenchmarkQueryPath/blocked_exact 55 allocs, 4214 B 55 allocs, 4214 B BenchmarkQueryPathLogLevel/info 55 allocs, 4211 B 55 allocs, 4209 B BenchmarkQueryPathLogLevel/trace 81 allocs, 7250 B 81 allocs, 7222 B

docs.title: Phase 3: remove avoidable per-query allocations
docs.text: Implement and benchmark one change at a time. Do not combine unrelated changes in a single measurement.

docs.title: Resolver race path
docs.text:
Targets in resolver/parallel_best_resolver.go:

  • make collectedErrors lazy: the successful first response should not create an error slice;
  • replace the small pickRandom result slice with a bounded stack-backed representation for the current resolver-count limits;
  • consider pooling the response channel only after ownership, draining, and cancellation rules are explicit. A channel must not return to the pool while a losing resolver can still send to it;
  • replace upstreamResolverStatus.lastErrorTime's atomic.Value containing a time.Time with an atomic.Int64 containing a monotonic nanosecond offset, if the benchmark confirms the load/store cost matters.

docs.title: Request and logging fields
docs.text:
Targets around server.newRequest:

  • retain UUID v7 semantics, but build the request logging fields lazily where possible;
  • calculate QuestionToString only when a Trace message is enabled;
  • avoid allocating secondary field maps for a disabled log line.

docs.title: Cache result path
docs.text:
Targets in cache/stringcache/in_memory_grouped_cache.go and the chained cache:

  • measure the single-group result path separately;
  • avoid a general-purpose map allocation when the caller needs only one known group, while preserving the public map[string]string contract at the API boundary;
  • keep the no-match path allocation-free;
  • verify that copy-on-write refreshes remain safe under concurrent lookup.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
• no semantic changes to resolver ordering, cancellation, retry, or error joining;
  • go test, non-e2e Ginkgo suites, and go test -race for touched packages;
  • allocation reduction demonstrated in Phase 1's complete query benchmark;
  • no regression in the existing parallel resolver benchmarks;
  • every optimization has a before/after table and a rollback point.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Phase 3 kept the resolver contracts unchanged while removing avoidable work from the parallel resolver path:

  • error collection is lazy, so a first successful response does not construct an error slice;
  • upstream error timestamps use an atomic.Int64 that holds a monotonic nanosecond offset (relative to a per-upstream clock base) instead of an atomic.Value containing a time.Time; the wall clock is no longer read, so a clock adjustment cannot distort the error window;
  • resolver status values are no longer copied when constructing success log fields, which avoids copying their atomic state.

A bounded-array rewrite of pickRandom was measured and then dropped: it did not change complete-path allocation counts, and compiler escape analysis confirmed that the existing selection slice is already stack-backed at the production call site after inlining. The simpler helper remains in place.

The final candidate was compared with the Phase 1 baseline using seven alternating A/B rounds, -benchtime=1s, and the same schedutil host. The complete-path allocation counts are unchanged: these changes remove work from paths that were not allocation-dominant in the Phase 1 fixtures, rather than changing the observable request allocation floor.

Measurement Phase 1 baseline Phase 3 Phase 3 delta BenchmarkChainLoggingPlumbing 109 allocs, 10152 B 109 allocs, 10152 B 0 allocs, 0 B BenchmarkQueryPath/upstream_hit 53 allocs, 4376 B 53 allocs, 4376 B 0 allocs, 0 B BenchmarkQueryPath/blocked_exact 55 allocs, 4214 B 55 allocs, 4214 B 0 allocs, 0 B BenchmarkQueryPath/upstream_miss 180 allocs, 15675 B 180 allocs, 15675 B 0 allocs, 0 B BenchmarkQueryPath/regex_only_miss 61 allocs, 5424 B 61 allocs, 5424 B 0 allocs, 0 B

The resolver-selection guardrail remained allocation-free on both sides. Timing differences are within the host's frequency noise; the exact allocation result is the important guardrail.

Raw Phase 3 output is retained under /tmp/opencode/bench/phase3-final2/.

docs.title: Existing behavior
docs.text: The grouped chain is constructed as regex, wildcard, string, and queried in reverse order. Therefore exact and wildcard matches already bypass the regex scan. This behavior is covered by the grouped-cache benchmark and must remain the first guardrail.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The remaining cost is the regex-only linear scan. The cache now performs a conservative required-literal analysis once, when a rule is inserted. It uses regexp/syntax only to inspect the pattern; matching continues to use the standard-library regexp.Regexp unchanged. A rule receives a filter literal only when that literal must occur, byte-for-byte and case-sensitively, in every possible match. Lookup first uses strings.Contains and calls Regexp.MatchString for every candidate that passes the filter.

The analyzer handles concatenation, captures, positive repetitions and positive bounded repetitions. It deliberately falls back to the normal regex scan for case-folded literals, alternation, optional or zero repetitions, character classes, assertions, arbitrary characters, malformed UTF-8 literals, parse failures, and unknown syntax operations. Thus an unclassified pattern has exactly the previous behavior; the filter can only skip a pattern that it has proved cannot match.

The pre-filter must never reject a pattern because of an incomplete parser or an assumption about regex syntax. Case sensitivity, anchors, escapes, alternation, Unicode, and empty matches need explicit tests.

docs.title: Classification rate
docs.text:
The fallback only costs something when a rule stays unclassified, so the question is how often that happens. Measured over the 209612 wildcard entries of helpertest/data/oisd-big-wildcard.txt, every rule in the shape a real OISD-derived regex list has (/^(.*\.)?<domain>$/) is classified - the domain literal is required in every match - so the fallback rate for that list shape is 0%.

The analyzer looks for a literal that must occur in every match, and a literal in one part of the pattern is enough even when another part is unclassified:

Pattern Required literal ^(.*\.)?example\.com$ example.com ^ads[0-9]+\.example\.com$ .example.com ^(ads\|analytics)\.example\.com$ .example.com ^example\.(com\|net)$ example. ^ad[sx]\.example\.com$ .example.com ^ads?\.example\.com$ .example.com .*ads.* ads (?i)^ads\.example\.com$ none (case-folded)

The rules that stay unclassified are the ones without a usable literal at all: case-insensitive patterns, patterns whose only literal parts are optional, and patterns built purely from character classes and assertions. A domain-blocking rule almost always contains a literal domain fragment, so the fallback rate of real configurations is low; it is high only for lists that are written as case-insensitive regexes.

docs.title: Measurement matrix
docs.text:
Run the standard-library regex benchmark with and without the pre-filter for:

  • OISD-shaped suffix rules;
  • literal-prefix rules;
  • arbitrary configured patterns;
  • 1, 10, 50, 100, 500, and 1000 rules;
  • first, middle, last, miss, near-miss, and short-domain queries;
  • exact and wildcard hits to prove they still do not enter the regex path.

docs.title: Correctness coverage
docs.text:
cache/stringcache/regex_cache_test.go now includes:

  • required-literal unit cases for anchors, escapes, Unicode, case folding, alternation, repetitions, and invalid patterns;
  • differential edge-case tests comparing ordered cache results with a plain regexp.Regexp scan, including mixed classified and fallback rules in both insertion orders;
  • fuzz seeds for fallback, Unicode, malformed UTF-8, empty-match, repetition, and escaped-literal patterns;
  • a direct check of every compiled rule in the real OISD-shaped fixture: for hit, near-hit, uppercase, suffix, and malformed-UTF-8 query variants, a non-empty filter is allowed to skip the rule only when MatchString also reports no match; and
  • zero-allocation checks for pre-filtered misses after cache construction.

The grouped-cache guardrails include exact-hit, wildcard-hit, and miss benchmarks. Exact and wildcard hits still short-circuit before the regex cache, while the benchmark's pre-filtered misses still check every cache without allocating. Unfiltered standard-library regex execution can allocate when its matching-state pool is empty, especially under the race detector.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The matrix was run against the Phase 3 state and the candidate in seven alternating A/B rounds. The Phase 4 matrix used -benchtime=100ms per sub-benchmark to cover all three pattern shapes, six rule counts, six query positions, and both implementations; the complete query-path and build measurements used the same alternating-round method. The table below shows the 1000-rule filtered cases; the standard scan is the standard sibling of every case and remains the semantic reference.

Pattern shape / query Standard ns/op Filtered ns/op Delta B/op standard / filtered allocs/op standard / filtered suffix / first 1267 1275 +0.6% 48 / 48 1 / 1 suffix / middle 489701 5452 -98.9% 48 / 48 1 / 1 suffix / last 1000657 9838 -99.0% 48 / 48 1 / 1 suffix / miss 1094059 13500 -98.8% 0 / 0 0 / 0 suffix / near-miss 1225149 16115 -98.7% 0 / 0 0 / 0 prefix / first 238 236 -0.9% 32 / 32 1 / 1 prefix / middle 43235 6015 -86.1% 32 / 32 1 / 1 prefix / last 83893 9009 -89.3% 32 / 32 1 / 1 prefix / miss 79973 15939 -80.1% 0 / 0 0 / 0 prefix / near-miss 92050 17576 -80.9% 0 / 0 0 / 0 fallback / first 1599 934 -41.6% 32 / 32 1 / 1 fallback / middle 137965 143397 +3.9% 32 / 32 1 / 1 fallback / last 283428 515574 +81.9% 32 / 32 1 / 1 fallback / miss 153589 214007 +39.3% 0 / 0 0 / 0

The first/near-miss standard values in the compact table can move with CPU frequency; the raw seven-round reports retain the exact medians and spreads. The complete matrix also covers 1, 10, 50, 100, and 500 rules plus the short query. Classified suffix and prefix rules show the intended large reduction when the match is late or absent.

Fallback rules are intentionally not classified, so they pay one extra branch per rule (required != "") and one wider cache entry (24 bytes instead of 8). The fallback rows of the table are dominated by the host's timing noise: six additional rounds of the 1000-rule fallback miss case produced 72.7-338.8 us for the standard scan and 80.8-189.9 us for the filtered scan, so the two distributions overlap completely. An isolated alternating A/B of the two cache representations, with the same 1000 case-insensitive rules and the same query, measured a median difference of +4.3%, +1.6% and -0.6% over three runs, which is about 3 ns per rule. The +81.9% of the fallback last-hit row is therefore not a systematic regression but the spread of the host's schedutil governor.

On the complete production query path, the real-list regex-only cases improved without changing allocation counts:

Case Base ns/op Candidate ns/op Delta B/op base / candidate allocs/op base / candidate BenchmarkQueryPath/regex_only_miss 1919695 63298 -96.7% 3568 / 3568 49 / 49 BenchmarkQueryPath/regex_late_hit 1219708 45856 -96.2% 3344 / 3421 50 / 50

Exact and wildcard paths remained separate guardrails. In the same run, blocked_exact was 3285 B / 49 allocs on both sides and blocked_wildcard was 3348 B / 50 allocs on both sides. The grouped-cache short-circuit benchmarks likewise kept exact hits at 336 B / 2 allocs and wildcard hits at 360 B / 3 allocs; their timing differences were within the host spread. The regex-only improvement therefore does not come from changing resolver ordering or making cheap cache hits enter the regex path.

The trade-off is paid at list load time. On the full real OISD-shaped regex fixture (BenchmarkRegexFactory, about 209k rules), the seven-round medians were:

Measurement Base Candidate Delta Build time 3.00 s 3.94 s +31.2% B/op 1.81 GB 2.16 GB +19.5% allocs/op 9.65 M 14.18 M +46.9%

The instrumented runs observed peak heap of approximately 440.9 MB for the base and 449.5 MB for the candidate. The retained/peak-memory increase is much smaller than the temporary allocation increase, but the startup cost is real and should be considered for frequent list reloads. The optimization is kept because query-time regex scans dominate steady-state workloads; the benchmark and the conservative fallback make the cost visible for future decisions.

Raw Phase 4 output is retained under /tmp/opencode/bench/phase4/.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
• differential results equal the standard-library-only implementation for all real list fixtures and generated edge cases;
  • no false negative is possible for an unclassified pattern;
  • regex-only miss and late-hit cases improve in the complete query benchmark;
  • compile time and memory are measured and documented as a list-loading trade-off;
  • the implementation continues to use the standard regexp package.

docs.title: Execution order and commits
docs.text:
The Go 1.27.3 and UUID migration is independent of the four performance phases. The direct UUID usage is submitted first as its own conventional commit:

build(go): use standard library UUID v7

That commit contains only the UUID import/API changes and changes the module requirement from direct to indirect. github.com/google/uuid remains in the module graph because github.com/oapi-codegen/runtime uses it transitively; it cannot be removed without changing that upstream dependency. This optimization plan and benchmark report remain documentation changes, not part of the UUID code commit.

After that migration:

  1. Phase 1: baseline benchmark and documentation;
  2. Phase 2: request logging plumbing (the lazy variant was evaluated and dropped, see the phase result);
  3. Phase 3: per-query allocation cuts;
  4. Phase 4: blocking regex pre-filter.

Each phase gets its own conventional commit, its own before/after benchmark table, and its own gofmt, build, vet, lint, test, and CodeQL validation. No alternative regex dependency is added unless a later benchmark disproves the current decision.

docs.title: Risk and rollback checklist
docs.text:
• Logging compatibility: compare golden output before and after Phase 2.
  • Cancellation: run race tests and stress losing parallel upstreams before pooling any channels.
  • Regex correctness: compare every pre-filter decision with standard regexp results and keep an explicit fallback path.
  • Memory: measure both Go heap allocations and retained process memory for large list loads.
  • Benchmark contamination: stop or wait for other compiles, rotate A/B order, and discard runs made on a busy host.
  • Rollback: each phase must be revertible without reverting the UUID migration or the established startup-performance commits.

docs.title: Regex engine benchmark
docs.text:
Historical engine comparison

These measurements predate the required-literal pre-filter and were not rerun for this branch. The selector and harness in the appendix are scratch code, not shipped build tags. See Query performance for the retained optimization.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The benchmark measured Denyzer's real regex path, not an isolated MatchString loop:

ChainedGroupedCache.Contains
  -> InMemoryGroupedCache.Contains
  -> regexCache.findMatch
  -> compiled regexp.MatchString

The benchmark-backed decision is:

  1. Do not replace the standard library with go-re2. Its default WASM implementation was usually slower on Denyzer's short domain strings and substantially slower for large OISD-shaped linear scans. Its re2_cgo mode requires a system-installed RE2 library through pkg-config, which does not fit the current Zig/musl cross-build setup.
  2. Do not make coregex a blanket replacement yet. It was dramatically faster for the OISD shape ^(.*\.)?domain$, but slower than the standard library for the literal-prefix shape after the first match. It also has materially higher compile cost and retained memory, and is pre-1.0.
  3. Keep regex work in Phase 4 (blocking regex pre-filter). First avoid entering the regex cache when exact or wildcard caches can decide the query. Then remeasure the remaining regex-only path. If an engine replacement is still justified, evaluate coregex only for the measured pattern class.

This report does not change the production regex implementation.

docs.title: Real cache-path benchmark
docs.text:
This test lives in cache/stringcache, so it can use the package's actual ChainedGroupedCache, InMemoryGroupedCache, regex factory, and OISD test data.

package stringcache

import (
    "fmt"
    "regexp"
    "runtime"
    "strings"
    "testing"

    engine "github.com/mia0x75/denyzer/internal/benchregexp"
)

// Patterns use the repository's actual OISD-derived data, in file order.
// Prefix patterns match the shape in grouped_cache_lookup_bench_test.go.
func enginePatterns(shape string, n int) ([]string, []string) {
    patterns, domains := make([]string, n), make([]string, n)
    for i := range n {
        if shape == "oisd" {
            patterns[i] = regexTestData[i]
            domains[i] = strings.TrimPrefix(wildcardTestData[i], "*.")
        } else {
            patterns[i] = fmt.Sprintf(`/^regex%d\..*$/`, i)
            domains[i] = fmt.Sprintf("regex%d.example.com", i)
        }
    }
    return patterns, domains
}

func engineChain(tb testing.TB, patterns []string) *ChainedGroupedCache {
    tb.Helper()
    c := NewChainedGroupedCache(
        NewInMemoryGroupedRegexCache(),
        NewInMemoryGroupedWildcardCache(),
        NewInMemoryGroupedStringCache(),
    )
    f := c.Refresh("default")
    for _, p := range patterns {
        if !f.AddEntry(p) {
            tb.Fatalf("entry rejected: %s", p)
        }
    }
    for i := range 200 {
        f.AddEntry(fmt.Sprintf("*.wild%d.example", i))
    }
    for i := range 5000 {
        f.AddEntry(fmt.Sprintf("string%d.example.com", i))
    }
    f.Finish()
    if got := c.ElementCount("default"); got != len(patterns)+5200 {
        tb.Fatalf("count %d", got)
    }
    return c
}

func BenchmarkEngineChain(b *testing.B) {
    for _, shape := range []string{"oisd", "prefix"} {
        for _, n := range []int{1, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000} {
            patterns, domains := enginePatterns(shape, n)
            c := engineChain(b, patterns)
            cases := []struct{ name, domain string }{
                {"first", domains[0]},
                {"middle", domains[n/2]},
                {"last", domains[n-1]},
                {"subdomain", "a.b.c." + domains[n-1]},
                {"miss", "not-present.example.org"},
                {"near-miss", domains[n-1] + ".invalid"},
                {"short-miss", "x.io"},
                {"exact", "string1234.example.com"},
                {"wildcard", "a.wild123.example"},
            }

            // Calculate the expected rule independently with the standard library.
            refs := make([]*regexp.Regexp, len(patterns))
            for i, p := range patterns {
                refs[i] = regexp.MustCompile(p[1 : len(p)-1])
            }
            for _, tc := range cases {
                want := ""
                for _, r := range refs {
                    if r.MatchString(tc.domain) {
                        want = "/" + r.String() + "/"
                        break
                    }
                }
                if tc.name == "exact" {
                    want = tc.domain
                }
                if tc.name == "wildcard" {
                    want = "*.wild123.example"
                }

                b.Run(fmt.Sprintf("%s/n=%d/%s", shape, n, tc.name), func(b *testing.B) {
                    groups := []string{"default"}
                    if got := c.Contains(tc.domain, groups)["default"]; got != want {
                        b.Fatalf("got %q want %q", got, want)
                    }
                    b.ReportAllocs()
                    b.ResetTimer()
                    for b.Loop() {
                        _ = c.Contains(tc.domain, groups)
                    }
                })
            }
        }
    }
}

func BenchmarkEngineCompile(b *testing.B) {
    for _, shape := range []string{"oisd", "prefix"} {
        for _, n := range []int{1, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000} {
            patterns, _ := enginePatterns(shape, n)
            b.Run(fmt.Sprintf("%s/n=%d", shape, n), func(b *testing.B) {
                b.ReportAllocs()
                for b.Loop() {
                    f := newRegexCacheFactory()
                    for _, p := range patterns {
                        if !f.addEntry(p) {
                            b.Fatal(p)
                        }
                    }
                    if f.count() != n {
                        b.Fatalf("compiled %d want %d", f.count(), n)
                    }
                    _ = f.create()
                }
            })
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Differential correctness and retained-memory checks
docs.text:
The correctness test compared every selected engine against the standard library. It also checked replacement behavior because util.Obfuscate uses ReplaceAllString.

func TestEngineDifferential(t *testing.T) {
    patterns, domains := enginePatterns("oisd", 1000)
    pp, dd := enginePatterns("prefix", 1000)
    patterns, domains = append(patterns, pp...), append(domains, dd...)
    patterns = append(patterns,
        `/.*google.com/`, `/^apple\.(de|com)$/`, `/amazon/`,
        `/(?i)example\.com$/`, `/^$/`, `/\bads\b/`, `/[a-zA-Z0-9]/`,
    )
    queries := []string{
        "", "x.io", "not-present.example.org", "EXAMPLE.COM", "apple.de",
        "www.google.com", "amazon", "ads.example", "例子.测试", "a\x00b",
    }
    for _, d := range domains {
        queries = append(queries, d, "a.b."+d, d+".invalid")
    }

    checks := 0
    for _, p := range patterns {
        p = p[1 : len(p)-1]
        ref, err := regexp.Compile(p)
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        got, err := engine.Compile(p)
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatalf("%s compile %q: %v", engine.Engine, p, err)
        }
        if got.String() != ref.String() {
            t.Fatalf("String mismatch %q", p)
        }
        for _, q := range queries {
            if a, b := got.MatchString(q), ref.MatchString(q); a != b {
                t.Fatalf("%s pattern=%q query=%q got=%v want=%v", engine.Engine, p, q, a, b)
            }
            checks++
        }
    }

    for _, p := range []string{"*", "?", "+", "[", "(wrongRegex", `\q`} {
        _, a := regexp.Compile(p)
        _, b := engine.Compile(p)
        if (a == nil) != (b == nil) {
            t.Fatalf("compile acceptance %q: %v / %v", p, a, b)
        }
    }
    for _, p := range []string{`[a-zA-Z0-9]`, `(example)`, `^|$`} {
        a, b := regexp.MustCompile(p), engine.MustCompile(p)
        for _, q := range queries[:10] {
            for _, replacement := range []string{"*", "$1", "${1}-x"} {
                if a.ReplaceAllString(q, replacement) != b.ReplaceAllString(q, replacement) {
                    t.Fatalf("replacement mismatch %q %q", p, q)
                }
            }
        }
    }
    t.Logf("engine=%s patterns=%d queries=%d match_checks=%d", engine.Engine, len(patterns), len(queries), checks)
}

func TestEngineRetainedMemory(t *testing.T) {
    for _, shape := range []string{"oisd", "prefix"} {
        for _, n := range []int{100, 500, 1000} {
            patterns, _ := enginePatterns(shape, n)
            runtime.GC()
            var before, after runtime.MemStats
            runtime.ReadMemStats(&before)
            f := newRegexCacheFactory()
            for _, p := range patterns {
                if !f.addEntry(p) {
                    t.Fatal(p)
                }
            }
            cache := f.create()
            runtime.ReadMemStats(&after)
            if cache == nil {
                t.Fatal("empty cache")
            }
            t.Logf("engine=%s shape=%s n=%d heap_delta=%d alloc_delta=%d",
                engine.Engine, shape, n,
                after.HeapAlloc-before.HeapAlloc,
                after.TotalAlloc-before.TotalAlloc)
            _ = cache
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Independent compile/RSS probe
docs.text:
The probe was built three times with the same selector tags. Running it as a separate process avoided retaining allocations from one engine or one regex count while measuring another.

package main

import (
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "runtime"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"

    "github.com/mia0x75/denyzer/internal/benchregexp"
)

func main() {
    n := flag.Int("n", 1000, "number of regexes")
    shape := flag.String("shape", "oisd", "pattern shape: oisd or prefix")
    flag.Parse()

    patterns := make([]string, *n)
    for i := range patterns {
        if *shape == "prefix" {
            patterns[i] = fmt.Sprintf(`^regex%d\..*$`, i)
        } else {
            patterns[i] = fmt.Sprintf(`^(.*\.)?domain%d\.example\.com$`, i)
        }
    }

    start := time.Now()
    compiled := make([]*benchregexp.Regexp, 0, len(patterns))
    for _, pattern := range patterns {
        r, err := benchregexp.Compile(pattern)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        compiled = append(compiled, r)
    }
    runtime.KeepAlive(compiled)

    var stats runtime.MemStats
    runtime.ReadMemStats(&stats)
    matched := false
    if len(compiled) > 0 {
        matched = compiled[len(compiled)-1].MatchString("a.domain999.example.com")
    }
    fmt.Printf(
        "engine=%s shape=%s n=%d compile_ns=%d heap_alloc=%d heap_sys=%d rss_kb=%d match=%v\n",
        benchregexp.Engine, *shape, *n, time.Since(start).Nanoseconds(),
        stats.HeapAlloc, stats.HeapSys, rssKB(), matched,
    )
}

func rssKB() int64 {
    data, err := os.ReadFile("/proc/self/status")
    if err != nil {
        return -1
    }
    for _, line := range strings.Split(string(data), "\n") {
        fields := strings.Fields(line)
        if len(fields) == 3 && fields[0] == "VmRSS:" {
            value, _ := strconv.ParseInt(fields[1], 10, 64)
            return value
        }
    }
    return -1
}

docs.title: Decision record: SQLite driver and release pipeline
docs.text:
Status

Accepted — the query log keeps the native SQLite driver and the release pipeline is built around it.

Date 2026-10-29 Decision Keep github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO), cross-compile with a Zig cc wrapper, build macOS on a macOS runner Alternatives modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go), ncruces/go-sqlite3 (WASM) Supersedes The inherited upstream configuration, which builds every target with CGO_ENABLED=0

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Denyzer stores its query log in an embedded SQLite database. The driver is github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3, the native (CGO) driver. The release configuration, however, was inherited from upstream Blocky and builds every target with CGO_ENABLED=0:

# .goreleaser.yml (before)
env:
  - CGO_ENABLED=0

That works for Blocky, whose SQLite support came from the pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite chain. For Denyzer it produces a binary that compiles, starts and even looks healthy — but the SQLite store is a non-functional stub:

Binary was compiled with 'CGO_ENABLED=0', go-sqlite3 requires cgo to work.
This is a stub

The query log silently falls back to the console writer, the dashboard shows an empty store and no release binary is actually able to do the job it is shipped for. The release pipeline therefore had to change one way or the other, and the only real question was whether to keep the native driver.

Two questions were open:

  1. Which driver should Denyzer use? The native driver is the fastest, but it forces CGO, and CGO costs the whole cross-compilation matrix.
  2. Can the native driver be cross-compiled for the complete release matrix? If not, the release matrix has to shrink or the release has to be produced on several platforms.

docs.title: Benchmark method
docs.text: The comparison was run with a throwaway harness that lives outside this repository and is not committed anywhere. It exists only to produce the numbers below and to validate the cross-compilation wrapper.

docs.title: Harness layout
docs.text:
run-all.sh              runs both benchmarks
run-drivers.sh          driver comparison only
drivers/                one Go module per driver
  benchcore/            shared workload, schema, cleanup and reporting
  mattn/                CGO driver, uses the exact production DSN
  modernc/              pure-Go transpiled driver
  ncruces/              pure-Go WASM driver
zigcc/
  cc-zig.sh             GOOS/GOARCH -> Zig triple wrapper
  matrix.sh             cross-compiles the probe for every release target
  probe/                minimal CGO program importing mattn/go-sqlite3
  shim/                 stub libresolv archives for the macOS probe
data/                   resulting database files (recreated per run)

The drivers cannot share one binary: mattn and ncruces both register the sqlite3 driver name, so each driver is a separate Go module with its own main.go and its own DSN syntax.

driver driver name busy timeout / WAL / sync syntax mattn sqlite3 ?_busy_timeout=5000&_journal_mode=WAL&... modernc sqlite ?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)&_pragma=... ncruces sqlite3 ?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)&_pragma=...

The mattn DSN is copied verbatim from storage/db.go, so it exercises the same pragmas that production uses: journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=NORMAL, txlock=immediate, cache_size=-65536 and mmap_size=256MiB.

docs.title: Workload
docs.text:
The workload is deliberately close to Denyzer's real shape:

  1. one transaction with a prepared INSERT into query_logs,
  2. followed by a COUNT(*) over a client prefix.

Both are what the asynchronous log writer and the dashboard reporting queries actually do. Each iteration creates a fresh database, inserts 500,000 rows and reads them back.

docs.title: Measurement rules
docs.text:
Run this on an otherwise idle machine

The numbers vary by a factor of three or more when other services are competing for disk and CPU. The harness reports the best and the median of N iterations so that a noisy run is at least visible, but the ordering of the drivers can flip on a loaded host.

The final run was taken on an idle host (load average 1.0 on 16 cores, no competing workloads, 25 GiB of free memory):

  • CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 5700U
  • Go: go1.26.10 linux/amd64
  • 10 iterations per driver, 500,000 rows per iteration

docs.title: Driver comparison (500k rows, 10 iterations, idle host)
docs.text:
driver median rows/s best rows/s spread median read mattn (CGO) 180226 205917 1.28x 47 ms ncruces (WASM) 159452 163708 1.11x 191 ms modernc (pure Go) 59312 62496 1.14x 113 ms

Relative to the median:

driver vs. modernc vs. mattn mattn (CGO) 3.04x 1.00x ncruces (WASM) 2.69x 0.88x modernc (pure Go) 1.00x 0.33x

All three drivers wrote the same 500,000 rows, returned the same 244,000 matching rows for the client-prefix count and produced byte-identical database files (28,610,560 bytes), so the comparison is like for like. The worst/best spread stays below 1.3x for every driver, so the ranking is reproducible rather than an artefact of the scheduler.

docs.title: What the numbers mean
docs.text:
• mattn (CGO) is the fastest, and it is also the fastest on reads (47 ms vs. 113 ms / 191 ms for the count query). It stays ahead of the pure-Go drivers on exactly the workload Denyzer performs.
  • ncruces is a viable pure-Go replacement — only about 12 % behind mattn on writes — but its read path is roughly 4x slower, which shows up on the dashboard's range scans and Top-N queries.
  • modernc is 3x slower than mattn on this workload. That is the driver upstream Blocky uses, and the reason the upstream release pipeline can build with CGO_ENABLED=0.

For Denyzer's actual traffic profile — a query log written in batches every 30 s, read by a dashboard that a human opens occasionally — the difference between 180k and 59k rows/s is not a bottleneck. The deciding factor is therefore not the raw write throughput but the release pipeline.

docs.title: Driver sizes (static binaries, -w -s)
docs.text:
build size mattn (CGO) 3.6 MiB modernc (pure Go) 5.4 MiB ncruces (pure Go) ~6 MiB

The native driver produces the smallest binary as well, because the transpiled pure-Go drivers carry a generated SQLite implementation.

docs.title: Cross-compilation matrix
docs.text:
The second benchmark cross-compiles a CGO program that imports github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 for every GOOS/GOARCH pair in Denyzer's release matrix, using the Zig wrapper:

linux/amd64       OK      windows/amd64     OK
linux/arm         OK      freebsd/amd64     OK
linux/arm64       OK      freebsd/arm       OK
linux/mipsle      OK      freebsd/arm64     OK
linux/mips        OK      netbsd/amd64      OK
linux/mips64le    OK      netbsd/arm        OK
linux/mips64      OK      netbsd/arm64      OK
openbsd/amd64     OK      darwin/amd64      linked*
openbsd/arm       OK      darwin/arm64      linked*
openbsd/arm64     OK

all targets built

* The two macOS rows only link in the harness, and they needed two extra hacks that are not part of the shipped wrapper — see "Why macOS is built on a macOS runner" below.

Zig ships a libc for the Linux (musl) and Windows (mingw) targets, so those binaries are self-contained: the Linux ones are statically linked, the Windows one imports nothing but the Universal CRT that Windows 10 and later ship. Zig has no libc for the BSDs, so those binaries are dynamically linked against the system libc (libc.so.7), like the binaries of the previous pure-Go releases.

The wrapper scripts/zigcc/cc-zig.sh translates GOOS/GOARCH/GOARM/GOMIPS into the matching Zig target triple and forwards the invocation to zig cc. It rejects macOS targets outright, so a cross build can never silently produce an unusable macOS binary.

docs.title: What the wrapper has to work around
docs.text: problem workaround Zig needs an explicit -target cc-zig.sh maps GOOS/GOARCH/GOARM/GOMIPS to a Zig triple Zig rejects -fno-PIC on the mips64 N64 ABI -Wno-error=option-ignored LLD rejects -Wl,-nopie and -Wl,--no-execute-only on BSD both flags are filtered out Go probes the linker with -fuse-ld=bfd on some targets and requires the output to contain GNU ld the probe is answered with a GNU ld version string and the flag is dropped from the real link

docs.title: Why macOS is built on a macOS runner
docs.text:
The two macOS rows are the reason the macOS cross builds were not accepted as a solution. In the harness they only linked, and only with two additional hacks: a stub libresolv archive had to be linked in, because Go's darwin runtime always links -lresolv, and -framework CoreFoundation had to be dropped, because Zig ships no macOS SDK. The resulting binary was never run on a real Mac, so the "OK" would have meant nothing more than "the linker did not complain".

A closer look confirmed that macOS cannot be cross-built from Linux at all. Go's darwin runtime always links -lresolv and imports the res_9_* symbols from /usr/lib/libresolv.9.dylib, a file that only exists on a real macOS host. The macOS binaries are therefore built on a macOS runner with the native Apple compiler, and the release workflow merges their archives into the release that the Linux job creates.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Keep github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO).

  1. It is the fastest driver for both the write and the read path.
  2. CGO_ENABLED=0 silently produces a non-functional binary with mattn (Binary was compiled with 'CGO_ENABLED=0', go-sqlite3 requires cgo to work. This is a stub), so the release configuration is broken and has to change anyway.
  3. The Zig cc wrapper cross-compiles the complete release matrix, so CGO does not cost the release matrix.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The release pipeline is built around the native driver:

  • .goreleaser.yml builds with CGO_ENABLED=1. The compiler comes from the CC environment variable, because GoReleaser has no dedicated cc field.
  • The release configuration contains two build groups that are selected with the DENYZER_TARGET environment variable:
  • cross (the default) — Linux, Windows and the BSDs, built through scripts/zigcc/cc-zig.sh.
  • darwin — macOS on Intel and Apple Silicon, built with the native clang on a macOS runner.
  • .github/workflows/release.yml builds the dashboard and runs unit tests first, then runs the Ubuntu cross build, the macos-latest build and the Docker build in parallel. Both GoReleaser jobs reuse the prepared dashboard and compile concurrently up to the runner's CPU count. Each smoke-test matrix waits only for its own build. Once all builds and tests pass, the final job uploads the macOS archives and merged checksums to the draft release created by the Linux job. Build artifacts expire after one day.
  • The container image is compiled on the target platform, because the SQLite driver needs the target's C toolchain. The non-native platforms are therefore emulated, which is why the release workflow sets up QEMU.
  • scripts/smoke-test.sh was added to prove that a release binary really talks to SQLite. It starts the server, resolves a name that is answered from the custom DNS mapping and reads the entry back through the API. A binary built without CGO fails this test, so the release matrix cannot silently regress into stub binaries again. The release workflow runs it on Linux amd64, arm64 and armv7, Windows amd64, and macOS amd64 and arm64, so a broken binary turns the workflow red before the draft is published by hand. ARMv6 is still built and published, but its smoke test is disabled because QEMU 10.2 exits with SIGILL before the server starts.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text:
If the release matrix ever has to be dropped, or the macOS builds can no longer be produced on a macOS runner, the fallback is github.com/ncruces/go-sqlite3: it is pure Go, needs no C toolchain, and costs about 12 % on the write path. Its DSN syntax differs from mattn's (?_pragma=... instead of ?_journal_mode=...), and the read path is about 4x slower, so the dashboard reporting queries would have to be revisited.

modernc.org/sqlite is not a viable fallback for Denyzer: it is 3x slower than mattn and, like the other pure-Go drivers, it would require rewriting the DSN and the schema handling in storage/db.go.

docs.title: Startup performance
docs.text: Denyzer prepares several independent things during startup: the denylist and the allowlist, every group inside each list, the resolvers of the query chain, and the configured upstreams. These stages used to run strictly one after another. They now run concurrently wherever they do not depend on each other, which cuts the time until the first query can be answered.

docs.title: What runs concurrently now
docs.text:
Stage Before After Denylist and allowlist loaded one after the other loaded concurrently List groups one group rebuilt at a time up to loading.groupConcurrency groups Query resolver components constructed one after the other independent components constructed concurrently Upstreams tested and initialised one by one upstreams of a group concurrently, groups concurrently

Only independent work is overlapped: the DNSSEC resolver still waits for the upstream tree, and client-name resolution still waits for custom DNS and the hosts file. A single list is never parsed by several goroutines, and the on-disk download cache (loading.downloads.cachePath) remains the way to speed up a single very large source.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Every stage compares a sequential reference with the concurrent production path:

  • sequential — the implementation before the change, kept in the test code as a reference implementation,
  • concurrent — the production path after the change. List-group benchmarks use groupConcurrency=1 and groupConcurrency=auto instead.

The two variants are run alternately (A, B, A, B, ...) so that a warm-up of one variant does not favour the other, and the median of the rounds is reported. Each benchmark round runs the operation -benchtime times.

Environment: AMD Ryzen 7 5700U (16 threads), Linux amd64, Go 1.26. The CPU frequency governor was left at the default schedutil. This matters: pinning all cores to the performance governor lets the package hit its power limit, which collapses multi-core throughput (the list-group benchmark below drops from 2.7x to 1.8x). The machine was otherwise idle; numbers on a busy host are higher in absolute terms and may scale differently.

docs.title: List loading
docs.text: List loading dominates startup on a typical configuration, so it is measured directly. Every iteration builds a fresh cache and parses the sources from disk, which is what happens at startup. Times are per operation; lower is better.

docs.title: Denylist and allowlist
docs.text:
One group with 100,000 entries per list (resolver, BenchmarkNewListCaches, -benchtime=10x, 3 rounds):

Mode Time sequential (before) 1307 ms concurrent (after) 686 ms

That is 1.9x faster, with identical allocations (about 40.6 MB, 1.4M allocs per operation) — the two caches simply overlap instead of adding up.

docs.title: List groups
docs.text:
100,000 entries per group (lists, BenchmarkNewListCacheMultiGroup, -benchtime=3x, 3 rounds). groupConcurrency: 1 is the sequential reference, auto is the new default:

Groups groupConcurrency: 1 (before) auto (default) Speedup 1 769 ms 287 ms ~1.0–2.7x (noisy) 2 1641 ms 967 ms 1.7x 4 2987 ms 1115 ms 2.7x

The default auto value is min(number of groups, max(1, loading.concurrency)), so the default source concurrency of 4 lets four groups load at once. Memory per operation is unchanged: the same entries are parsed, only the number of caches alive at the same moment changes (about 10 MB per 100,000-entry group).

docs.title: Query chain construction
docs.text:
server, BenchmarkNewQueryResolverParts, -benchtime=10x, 3 rounds. The benchmark builds the query chain components with a slow list source and a slow mock upstream (200 ms each), so it reflects the I/O-bound startup work:

Mode Time sequential (before) 409 ms concurrent (after) 208 ms

That is 2.0x faster. The concurrent construction runs in two stages: the independent components (upstream tree, blocking, query logging, conditional upstream, hosts file, caching resolver) are built at the same time, and the components that depend on them (client names, DNSSEC) are built afterwards.

docs.title: Upstream initialization
docs.text:
resolver, -benchtime=10x, 3 rounds. Four mock upstreams answer the initialization test query after 25 ms, so the benchmarks measure how well the initialization is parallelized:

Benchmark sequential (before) concurrent (after) Speedup BenchmarkCreateGroupResolvers (4 upstreams in one group) 102 ms 26 ms 4.0x BenchmarkCreateUpstreamBranches (4 groups) 102 ms 26 ms 4.0x

Both the upstreams inside a group and the groups themselves are initialised concurrently. The configured order of upstreams within each group is preserved, because the strict strategy depends on it. Group names are map keys, not an ordered sequence.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
go test ./resolver/ -run '^$' -bench BenchmarkNewListCaches -benchtime=10x -count=3
go test ./lists/    -run '^$' -bench BenchmarkNewListCacheMultiGroup -benchtime=3x -count=3
go test ./server/   -run '^$' -bench BenchmarkNewQueryResolverParts -benchtime=10x -count=3
go test ./resolver/ -run '^$' -bench 'BenchmarkCreateGroupResolvers|BenchmarkCreateUpstreamBranches' -benchtime=10x -count=3

The benchmarks compare the reference implementation with the production implementation, so the numbers can be reproduced without checking out an older commit. To alternate A/B rounds, run each sub-benchmark separately; -count alone repeats each variant before moving to the next. Run them on an otherwise idle machine and keep the CPU frequency governor at schedutil.
